This application-based exercise bridges the gap between pure legal definitions and tactical decision-making, ensuring students leave with a robust, visual understanding of federal tax administration.

tasks: Determine when the IRS can audit beyond the standard three-year limitation.
Identify judicial routes for resolving disputed tax determinations.

sessions.title: Filing Status and Dependents
sessions.description: Review criteria for filing statuses and qualifying child/relative dependencies.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by mapping out the five filing statuses on the left side of our board, establishing that filing status is not merely an administrative checkbox but the fundamental filter that dictates tax rates, standard deductions, and phase-out thresholds. The primary goal is to guide students through the hierarchy of statuses—Single, Married Filing Jointly (MFJ), Married Filing Separately (MFS), Head of Household (HOH), and Qualifying Surviving Spouse (QSS, historically Qualifying Widow/Widower). Highlight that the IRS looks at a taxpayer's marital status as of December 31st of the tax year; a common pitfall is thinking a mid-year divorce is prorated. Introduce a timeline schematic to visualize how a transition occurs, emphasizing how filing status impacts the standard deduction. 

Transitioning to the Qualifying Surviving Spouse (QSS) status, map out a clear timeline to clear up the widespread confusion regarding the 'two-year' rule. Draw a timeline showing Year 0 (the year the spouse dies) and subsequent years. On Year 0, the surviving spouse can still file MFJ (assuming they haven't remarried). For Year 1 and Year 2, they may qualify for QSS, which grants them the same favorable tax brackets and standard deduction as MFJ. We must emphasize the strict qualifying criteria on our whiteboard: the taxpayer must remain unmarried, must pay over half the cost of maintaining a household, and must have a dependent child (son, daughter, stepson, or stepdaughter) living with them for the *entire* tax year. A crucial trap to highlight is the distinction between a 'dependent child' and other relatives—QSS specifically requires a biological, adopted, or stepchild, whereas other statuses have broader definitions. Use a quick scenario-based check on the board: if the spouse passed away in 2022, write out the status for 2022 (MFJ), 2023 (QSS), 2024 (QSS), and 2025 (HOH or Single), ensuring students visualize the exact transition points.

Next, draw a dividing line on the whiteboard to transition into dependency exemptions, which now serve as the structural backbone for various tax credits and filing eligibility. Introduce the two main categories: Qualifying Child (QC) and Qualifying Relative (QR). We will construct a comparative matrix on the board to pit these two against each other across four critical dimensions: Relationship, Age/Support, Residency/Income, and Joint Return limitations. This visual contrast is the most effective way to prevent students from mixing up the rules. Explain that for a QC, we use the 'CARES' acronym (Close Relative, Age Limit, Residency, Eliminate Gross Income Test, Support Test). Walk through each: the child must live with the taxpayer for more than half the year (Residency), must be under 19 (or under 24 if a full-time student), and must not have provided more than half of their *own* support (note the pedagogical nuance: the taxpayer does not have to provide over half the support, the child just must not provide over half of their own). 

Now, introduce the 'SUPORT' acronym on the board for Qualifying Relatives, which applies when a dependent does not meet the QC criteria. Detail the requirements: Support (taxpayer must provide over 50% of support), Under gross income limit (taxpayer's gross taxable income must be under a highly specific inflation-adjusted threshold), Precludes filing a joint return, Only US citizens/residents, Relative test OR Taxpayer lives with the individual for the entire year. Highlight the 'Gross Income' test as a major pitfall area—unlike QC, which has no gross income limit for the dependent, a QR must have gross income below the statutory limit. Additionally, clarify the 'Relative or Member of Household' rule: a true relative does not need to live with the taxpayer for the entire year to qualify, but a non-relative must live in the household for all 365 days. 

Conclude the session with a live diagnostic flow chart exercise. Present a scenario where a taxpayer supports their 25-year-old cousin who earned $3,000 but lived with them for only 9 months. Walk students through the decision tree: Is the cousin a Qualifying Child? No, because they fail the age test and relationship test. Is the cousin a Qualifying Relative? Let's check: the taxpayer provided over half the support, the income is below the limit, but because a cousin is not considered a 'relative' under the strict IRS definition, they must live with the taxpayer for the *entire* year. Since they only lived there for 9 months, they fail. This practical application cements the precise boundaries of tax law and prepares students for complex simulation scenarios where subtle facts dictate massive tax differences.

tasks: Determine the optimal filing status for a qualifying widow(er).
Apply support and relationship tests for dependency determinations.

sessions.title: Gross Income
sessions.description: Calculate taxable income items, identifying specific exclusions like gifts, life insurance, and municipal bond interest.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing the foundational concept of the 'All-Inclusive Income Concept' under Internal Revenue Code Section 61, which states that gross income means all income from whatever source derived unless specifically excluded. On the whiteboard, draw a massive container representing total economic benefit. Explain to the candidates that the default position of the IRS is that every dollar, service, or bartered item entering this container is taxable. This concept-first visualization helps candidates understand that they should not look for reasons to include an item in gross income, but rather look for specific, statutory provisions that allow for exclusion. This shifts their mental model from memorizing a list of taxable items to identifying the narrow gates of exclusions. 

Next, we transition to the specific exclusions that frequently test a candidate's precision on the CPA exam: gifts, life insurance proceeds, and municipal bond interest. On the whiteboard, draw three distinct 'shields' outside of our gross income container. Explain that gifts and inheritances are excluded because they are taxed under a separate transfer tax regime, not the income tax regime. For life insurance, illustrate how proceeds paid by reason of the death of the insured are generally excluded to prevent taxing a safety net, but highlight a high-frequency pitfall: if the policy was transferred for valuable consideration, the exclusion is lost, and only the investment amount remains tax-free. For municipal bond interest, map out the flow of interest from state and local obligations, contrasting it with fully taxable federal treasury interest to prevent the common mistake of treating all government bonds equally.

Now, we dive into the complex and highly-tested rules of alimony. Draw a timeline on the whiteboard dividing agreements before December 31, 2018, and those on or after January 1, 2019. For pre-2019 agreements, map out the symmetrical tax treatment: alimony is deductible to the payor (above-the-line) and taxable to the recipient. For post-2018 agreements, show how the tax system completely ignores the transfer: it is non-deductible to the payor and non-taxable to the recipient. To reinforce this, we will run through a quick practice scenario where a divorce decree executed in 2017 is modified in 2020. This exercise is designed to reveal whether learners can distinguish when a modification legally triggers the new tax rules versus when it preserves the grandfathered status.

Following alimony, we dissect employee fringe benefits. On the board, draw a spectrum ranging from fully taxable compensation to statutory non-taxable benefits. Focus on common employer-provided benefits such as group term life insurance, where only the coverage exceeding $50,000 creates a taxable constructive benefit calculated using IRS premium tables. Walk through a visualization of an employee receiving $150,000 of coverage, showing how the first $50,000 is shielded, and the premium for the remaining $100,000 must be calculated and added to their gross income. This concrete example prevents students from incorrectly assuming the entire benefit is either fully taxable or fully tax-free.

Finally, we tackle the multi-tiered calculation of taxable Social Security benefits. This is notoriously difficult for candidates because it is determined using a sliding scale based on 'Modified Adjusted Gross Income' (MAGI) plus half of the taxpayer's Social Security benefits. On the whiteboard, construct a step-by-step formula showing how to calculate this base. Then, draw three horizontal bands representing the taxability thresholds: 0%, up to 50%, and up to 85% of the benefits. Explain that the formula is designed to tax wealthier retirees while keeping low-income retirees tax-free. Walk through a computational scenario of a married couple with modest retirement income, demonstrating how to compute their MAGI and map it against the statutory thresholds. This structured mathematical workflow demystifies the calculation and equips candidates to handle multi-step simulation questions on the exam.

tasks: Determine taxable and excludable components of alimony and fringe benefits.
Calculate taxable social security benefits based on modified AGI.

sessions.title: Adjustments and Deductions
sessions.description: Distinguish above-the-line adjustments (for AGI) from below-the-line itemized deductions (from AGI) or standard deductions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by drawing a massive, vertical, double-ruled line representing Adjusted Gross Income (AGI)—the single most critical dividing line in individual income taxation. Under a concept-first public lecture style, we present this not as a collection of dry rules, but as an elegant multi-step logical funnel. Everything above this line consists of adjustments 'for' AGI, which are highly beneficial because they reduce gross income directly without being subject to phase-outs or floors tied to a percentage of AGI. Everything below this line consists of deductions 'from' AGI, where taxpayers must choose between the standard deduction or itemized deductions. Visualizing this threshold is crucial because a lower AGI unlocks many other tax benefits, making 'above-the-line' deductions inherently more valuable than 'below-the-line' ones.

Next, we transition to the mechanics of above-the-line adjustments, focusing specifically on the student loan interest deduction to demonstrate the concept of phase-outs. The teacher should write down a clear formula on the whiteboard illustrating how a benefit is systematically restricted as a taxpayer's modified AGI (MAGI) climbs. We present a dynamic scenario: a single taxpayer earning just over the threshold, and we show how to calculate the phase-out fraction. A common student pitfall is applying the phase-out ratio directly to the total interest paid rather than first capping the deductible interest at the statutory limit. We walk through the exact steps of establishing the raw deduction, calculating the phase-out fraction based on the MAGI range, and subtracting the phased-out portion to arrive at the final allowed adjustment.

Moving below the AGI line, we construct the medical expense deduction framework on the whiteboard to illustrate the concept of a tax 'floor.' Unlike phase-outs which penalize high income by reducing deductions, floors act as hurdles where only the portion of expenses exceeding a certain percentage of AGI is deductible. We draw a ledger of typical medical expenses—including prescription drugs, health insurance premiums, and doctor visits—while explicitly crossing off non-deductible items like cosmetic surgery or over-the-counter vitamins to preempt common classification errors. We then apply the percentage floor to show how the deduction is calculated, proving to students that a higher AGI raises this hurdle and effectively shrinks their itemized medical deduction.

To close the session, we run a comparative walkthrough comparing a taxpayer's total itemized deductions against the standard deduction threshold. We draw a side-by-side balancing scale on the whiteboard to demonstrate how taxpayers decide whether to itemize. By showing how medical expenses, state and local taxes (SALT) capped at their statutory limits, and mortgage interest combine, students will visualize the tipping point where itemizing becomes more beneficial than taking the standard deduction. This conceptual anchoring ensures that students understand not just how to calculate individual lines, but how these components interact dynamically within the entire individual tax formula.

tasks: Calculate deductible medical expenses based on AGI limits.
Compute student loan interest phase-out calculations.

sessions.title: Tax Credits
sessions.description: Explore child tax credits, child and dependent care credits, education credits, and refundable vs. nonrefundable classifications.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core conceptual hurdle in the world of tax credits: understanding the mechanical difference between a tax deduction and a tax credit, and specifically, the distinction between refundable and nonrefundable credits. On the whiteboard, draw a simple two-column flowchart. The first column illustrates how deductions reduce taxable income before tax rates are applied (saving a fraction of the dollar depending on the tax bracket), while the second column demonstrates how credits reduce the tax liability dollar-for-dollar. Beneath this, split the credit column into 'Nonrefundable' (which can reduce the tax bill to zero but no further) and 'Refundable' (which can generate a refund check even if the tax liability is zero). This structural visualization prevents the common student pitfall of treating credits as mere deductions and highlights why refundable credits are highly prized.

Next, we transition to the Child and Dependent Care Credit, focusing on the mechanics of its calculation. Teachers should write the formula on the whiteboard, detailing the eligible expense limits ($3,000 for one qualifying individual, $6,000 for two or more) and how these expenses must be supported by earned income (taking the lesser of taxpayer or spouse's earned income). Introduce a scenario where one spouse has high earnings and the other has $2,000 of part-time income, showing how the credit base is restricted to that lower amount. This prevents the common mistake of automatically applying the maximum limit without checking the earned income constraint. Work through the phase-out mechanism, demonstrating how the credit percentage scales down from 35% to 20% as Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) increases, explaining why this credit is technically nonrefundable but highly structured to target lower-income individuals.

Following this, draw a side-by-side comparison matrix on the whiteboard to contrast the two primary education tax credits: the American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC) and the Lifetime Learning Credit (LLC). For the AOTC, emphasize that it is only available for the first four years of post-secondary education, has a maximum credit of $2,500 per student (calculated as 100% of the first $2,000 and 25% of the next $2,000 of qualified expenses), and possesses a unique hybrid nature—being 40% refundable (up to $1,000). For the LLC, highlight that it is available for an unlimited number of years, covers graduate courses or job skills courses, provides a maximum credit of $2,000 per tax return (calculated as 20% of up to $10,000 of qualified expenses), and is completely nonrefundable.

Conclude the session with a brief diagnostic check. Present the students with a hypothetical family that has one child in college (first year) and another child in graduate school, with a set amount of qualified tuition expenses for both. Walk through the decision-making process of assigning the AOTC to the undergraduate student and the LLC to the graduate student on the board. This real-time synthesis helps students see how to maximize education tax benefits across different family members, solidifying their understanding of phase-outs, eligibility criteria, and the structural differences between these two high-frequency exam topics.

tasks: Calculate child and dependent care credit limits.
Distinguish the American Opportunity Tax Credit from the Lifetime Learning Credit.

sessions.title: Property Basis
sessions.description: Calculate basis for purchases, inherited property, gifted property, and conversions to business use.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by establishing the fundamental concept of 'basis' on the whiteboard. Instead of treating basis as a dry, mechanical number, we define it conceptually as a taxpayer's tax-free recovery of capital—essentially, a running ledger of after-tax dollars invested in an asset. Under the simple rule of purchased property, basis is straightforwardly equal to cost. However, the true complexity of the CPA exam lies in transactions where property is acquired without a direct purchase. We draw a primary division on the board separating transfers during life (inter vivos gifts) from transfers at death (testamentary inheritances), setting up the core intellectual tension of the session: why the tax code treats these two pathways radically differently.

Next, we construct a comprehensive decision tree on the whiteboard to tackle the complex dual-basis rules for gifted property. We start with the general rule: the donee assumes the donor's adjusted basis (a carryover basis). But then we introduce the exception that trips up many candidates—when the fair market value (FMV) at the date of the gift is lower than the donor's adjusted basis. We illustrate this visually with parallel tracks on the board labeled 'Gain Basis' (equal to the donor's adjusted basis) and 'Loss Basis' (equal to the lower FMV on the gift date). We explain the regulatory logic behind this dual-basis rule: the IRS designs these mechanics to prevent taxpayers from shifting built-in personal losses to other individuals with higher tax brackets. 

To make this concrete, we map out three distinct selling price scenarios on the board to show how the donee's realized gain or loss is derived. Scenario one shows a sale price higher than the donor's basis, resulting in a gain calculated using the donor's basis. Scenario two shows a sale price lower than the gift-date FMV, resulting in a loss calculated using the lower FMV. Scenario three is the 'no gain, no loss' zone, where the selling price falls directly between the donor's basis and the FMV; we visually highlight how the basis defaults to the sales price itself, erasing any tax consequence. Alongside this, we detail the holding period tracking rules. We show that if the carryover basis is used, the donor's holding period 'tacks on' to the donee's ownership; if the FMV (loss basis) is used, the holding period starts anew on the day after the gift. A common student pitfall is automatically tacking on the holding period in loss situations, which we actively debunk here.

We then transition the whiteboard focus to inherited property, drawing a sharp contrast against the gift rules. We write 'Step-Up to FMV' in bold letters. Under Section 1014, the general rule is that the heir's basis becomes the FMV of the property at the date of the decedent's death. We also introduce the Alternate Valuation Date (AVD) option, noting that if elected by the executor, the basis becomes the FMV six months after death (or the date of distribution, if earlier). Crucially, we emphasize a unique, highly tested rule on the whiteboard: inherited property is automatically granted a long-term holding period, regardless of how long the decedent actually owned the asset or how quickly the heir sells it. We explain the policy intent here—alleviating the administrative burden on grieving families who might otherwise have to search for historical purchase records spanning decades.

Finally, we cover the conversion of personal-use property to business-use property. We draw a comparison to the gift dual-basis rule, explaining that when personal property is converted to business use, its basis for depreciation and loss is the lesser of the taxpayer's adjusted basis or the FMV at the date of conversion. This prevents taxpayers from converting personal depreciation and decline in value into deductible business losses. We conclude the whiteboard session with a comprehensive, multi-part practice problem. We present a scenario where an individual receives a gift of stock, holds it briefly, and sells it, alongside an inheritance of real estate sold shortly after death. We walk through the step-by-step derivations of the gain, loss, and holding periods, asking students to identify which basis applies at each decision node to ensure they can confidently apply these rules under exam pressure.

tasks: Calculate the donor's basis, donee's basis, and realized gain/loss on a gift sale.
Determine basis adjustments for inherited property.

sessions.title: Property Dispositions
sessions.description: Compare capital and ordinary gains, Section 1231 transactions, depreciation recapture, and non-taxable exchange structures.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by structuring the grand taxonomy of property dispositions. Students often get overwhelmed by the overlapping labels of capital assets, ordinary assets, and Section 1231 assets. To anchor their understanding, we draw a massive three-column matrix on the board. The first column outlines ordinary assets (primarily inventory and accounts receivable arising from daily business operations), the second represents capital assets (held for investment or personal use, governed by Section 1221), and the third introduces Section 1231 assets (depreciable personal property and real property held for use in a trade or business for more than one year). The core pedagogical goal here is to help students appreciate why Section 1231 is the 'best of both worlds'—granting capital gain treatment on net gains, but ordinary loss treatment on net losses. We visually highlight this asymmetric tax benefit to demonstrate how Congress incentivizes business investment.

Next, we transition to the critical mechanics of depreciation recapture under Sections 1245 and 1250. This is a high-frequency pitfall zone where candidates often mistakenly apply capital gains rates to accumulated depreciation. On the whiteboard, we write out a clear timeline of a machine's lifecycle: its initial purchase, depreciation deductions that reduced ordinary income in prior years, and its eventual sale at a gain. We explain that because the depreciation deductions offset ordinary income at high rates, the IRS demands that any gain on sale up to that accumulated depreciation must be recaptured as ordinary income under Section 1245. We walk through a numerical example: a machine bought for $10,000, depreciated down to $4,000, and sold for $11,000. We map out the $7,000 total gain, demonstrating how the first $6,000 is recaptured as Section 1245 ordinary income (equal to the depreciation taken), while the remaining $1,000 is treated as Section 1231 gain. For Section 1250, we briefly whiteboard the concept of unrecaptured Section 1250 gains for real property, clarifying that for individuals, this is taxed at a maximum rate of 25% rather than standard capital gain rates, which prevents them from bypassing real estate recapture limits.

From recapture, we pivot to the logic of non-taxable exchange structures, specifically focusing on Section 1031 Like-Kind Exchanges. We start by asking a conceptual question to prompt the underlying logic: 'If you trade one office building for another without receiving cash, do you actually have the liquidity to pay tax?' This intuitive question introduces the concept of continuity of investment and the deferral of gain. We draw a flow diagram of a standard like-kind transaction. We define 'boot' as any non-like-kind property or cash received in the transaction and highlight the golden rule: gain is recognized only to the lesser of the realized gain or the boot received. We warn students against a common trap: assuming that liabilities assumed by the other party act as boot received, which is true, but they can be offset by liabilities assumed by the taxpayer. We map out this net liability relief concept directly on the board.

We conclude with a comprehensive, step-by-step whiteboard calculation of both recognized gain and deferred basis in a like-kind exchange. We write down the two central formulas side-by-side: Basis of New Property = Adjusted Basis of Property Given + Gain Recognized - Boot Received, and its mathematical equivalent, Basis of New Property = Fair Market Value of Property Received - Deferred Gain. By showing both formulas, we help students verify their calculations and build mathematical intuition. We run through a practice scenario where a taxpayer exchanges real property with an adjusted basis of $150,000 for like-kind real property with an FMV of $200,000 and receives $30,000 cash (boot). We calculate the realized gain ($230,000 total value received minus $150,000 basis equals $80,000 realized), the recognized gain (the $30,000 boot received, which is less than the $80,000 realized gain), and the final deferred basis ($150,000 basis + $30,000 recognized - $30,000 boot received = $150,000). We visually highlight how the deferred gain of $50,000 ($80,000 realized minus $30,000 recognized) is embedded in the new property's basis ($200,000 FMV minus $150,000 basis), cementing their grip on tax deferral mechanics.

tasks: Perform Section 1245 and 1250 depreciation recapture calculations.
Determine recognized gain and deferred basis in a like-kind exchange.

lectures.title: Federal Taxation of Entities
lectures.description: Focuses on entity taxation, examining tax formations, operations, and liquidations for corporations, partnerships, estates, and tax-exempt organizations.

sessions.title: C Corporations
sessions.description: Formulate tax adjustments, book-to-tax reconciliations (Schedule M-1/M-3), and Section 351 formation transactions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by setting up a clear visual split on the whiteboard: one side represents the corporate entity as an independent legal tax bubble, and the other represents its contributors. This conceptual starting point is vital because it explains why Section 351 exists. Instead of treating the contribution of appreciated property to a new corporation as a taxable sale, tax law allows for a deferral of gain to encourage business formation. On the board, sketch out the three-part 'Section 351 Control Club' test: property must be transferred, solely in exchange for stock, and the transferors must collectively hold at least 80% of the total voting power and total shares immediately after the exchange. We must call out the classic trap where services are contributed instead of property; write 'Services = Taxable Income at Fair Market Value' in red on the board, demonstrating how a service partner's shares can break the 80% control threshold for everyone else if not structured carefully.

Next, expand the whiteboard visual to show how basis is computed under Section 351 when 'boot' (cash or non-qualifying property) enters the equation. Draw a horizontal pipeline showing how the shareholder’s basis in the newly acquired stock is derived from their adjusted basis in the contributed property, plus any gain recognized, minus any boot received or liabilities assumed by the corporation. Directly below this, draw the corresponding corporation's inside basis calculation. Show that the corporation takes the shareholder's transfer basis plus any gain the shareholder had to recognize. Address the psychological hurdle students face with liability assumption under Section 357: explain that while liabilities assumed by the corporation generally reduce shareholder basis, they trigger a recognized gain if they exceed the total adjusted basis of all properties transferred. This prevents negative basis, which is an arithmetic impossibility in tax law.

Transition the whiteboard layout to focus on the bridge between financial accounting and tax compliance: the Schedule M-1 and M-3 reconciliations. Draw a large T-chart titled 'Book-to-Tax Adjustments'. On the left, list temporary differences—items that impact both book and tax but in different periods, such as MACRS vs. straight-line depreciation, warranty liabilities, and bad debt reserves. On the right, list permanent differences—items that are recognized for either book or tax but never both, such as tax-exempt municipal interest, non-deductible fines, and life insurance premiums where the corporation is the beneficiary. Walk through the mathematical sign of each adjustment. Emphasize that to go from book income to taxable income, we must add back expenses that are non-deductible for tax purposes and subtract income items that are non-taxable, reversing this logic for taxable income items not captured in book revenue.

Now, introduce the mechanics of the Dividends Received Deduction (DRD), which exists to prevent triple taxation of the same corporate earnings. On the board, draw a pyramid divided into three tiers: a 50% deduction for ownership under 20%, a 65% deduction for ownership between 20% and 80%, and a 100% deduction for ownership of 80% or more. Introduce the multi-step calculation sequence: first, calculate tentative DRD based on the dividend received; second, calculate the taxable income limitation; and third, apply the crucial 'NOL exception' loophole. Explain that if taking the full tentative DRD creates or increases a Net Operating Loss (NOL) for the corporation, the taxable income limitation is completely bypassed, allowing the corporation to claim the full deduction. This is a notorious high-frequency exam pitfall that requires a step-by-step mathematical walkthrough on the board.

Conclude the session with an active whiteboard diagnostic walkthrough of a comprehensive problem that fuses these concepts. Present a hypothetical corporation with a starting book income, several M-1 adjustment items (such as entertainment expenses, municipal bond interest, and depreciation differences), and a dividend received from a 15%-owned domestic corporation. Ask the students to first identify which differences are permanent versus temporary, adjust the book income to find taxable income before the DRD, and then test both DRD scenarios—one where the limitation applies, and one where the loss exception is triggered. By writing out the math side-by-side, students will visually witness how the DRD limitation disappears when the corporation is pushed into a net operating loss, solidifying their computational and strategic exam intuition.

tasks: Complete a Schedule M-1 reconciliation for temporary and permanent differences.
Calculate corporate tax liability, taking into account dividend exclusions.

sessions.title: S Corporations
sessions.description: Analyze eligibility requirements, election mechanics, allocation rules, and shareholder basis adjustments.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by framing S Corporations as a powerful hybrid tax entity. In a concept-first style, we introduce S Corps as standard legal corporations that have made a special election to be taxed as pass-through entities. This means we avoid the double taxation of C Corporations while retaining the corporate shield. To make this concrete, draw a simple split screen on the board: on the left, a standard C Corp paying corporate-level tax and distributing taxed dividends; on the right, an S Corp where profits flow directly to the owners' tax returns without an intermediate tax layer. Explain that because this is a highly advantageous tax status, the IRS guards the gates fiercely. This framing helps students understand why the strict eligibility criteria exist: they prevent complex multinational structures from exploiting this simplified pass-through regime.

Next, list the specific eligibility hurdles on the board as a checklist. We must systematically go through each rule: the corporation must be domestic, have no more than 100 shareholders, allow only individual, estate, or certain trust shareholders, and have only one class of stock. We will visually group 'eligible shareholders' vs. 'ineligible shareholders' (such as partnerships, corporations, and non-resident aliens) to build instant recognition. A critical teaching point here is the 'one class of stock' rule. Explain that while differences in common stock voting rights are perfectly acceptable, any difference in dividend rights or liquidation preferences will immediately blow the election. Ask the students a conceptual question: if a corporation issues Class A voting stock and Class B non-voting stock, does this violate the S Corp rules? Draw out the distinction that voting rights do not create a second class of stock, preventing a common trap where candidates conflate voting rights with economic rights.

Now, transition to the mechanics of S Corporation elections and terminations. Draw a calendar timeline on the board to illustrate the critical timing of IRS Form 2553. If an entity wants S Corp status to be effective for the current taxable year, it must file the election by the 15th day of the third month of that year. Show that any election filed after this window defaults to being effective for the following tax year. Then, explain how an S Corp status can be terminated voluntarily (requiring consent from shareholders holding more than 50% of the stock) or involuntarily (by failing any eligibility criteria mid-year). Draw a line dividing a single tax year into an S short year and a C short year to show how income must be allocated when status is terminated mid-year.

We then move to the operational phase: how S Corporations allocate income and how shareholders track their investment. Unlike partnerships, S Corporations must allocate income and losses strictly on a pro-rata, per-share, per-day basis. Write out the allocation formula on the board: (Total Income) x (Shareholder's Ownership %) x (Days Owned / 365). Use a quick example of a shareholder who sells their 50% stake halfway through the year. This strict allocation rule exists because S Corporations cannot utilize the flexible 'special allocations' allowed in partnership agreements. Highlighting this fundamental rigidness helps candidates transition smoothly between S Corps and Partnership modules.

Next, dedicate a large section of the whiteboard to S Corporation Shareholder Basis. This is the most heavily tested area and where conceptual clarity is paramount. Introduce basis not just as a compliance number, but as an ongoing tracker of previously taxed money. Write out the strict basis adjustment ordering sequence on the board. Start at the top with Beginning Basis, then add contributions and ordinary/separately stated income items. Crucially, show that tax-exempt income increases basis. Next, subtract distributions that are not dividend distributions. Finally, subtract non-deductible expenses and then deductible losses. Emphasize why the ordering rule matters: distributions are assessed for taxability before losses are deducted. If a distribution exceeds basis, it triggers capital gains. If a loss exceeds remaining basis, it is suspended and carried forward indefinitely.

To solidify this, run through a diagnostic walkthrough exercise on the board. Lay out a scenario: a shareholder starts with $10,000 basis, receives a tax-free distribution of $12,000, and is allocated a $5,000 loss. Walk through the math step-by-step. Show how the $12,000 distribution first reduces the basis to $0, creating a $2,000 taxable capital gain, and leaves the $5,000 loss suspended because the basis is already exhausted. Conclude by addressing a massive pitfall: unlike partnerships, S Corporation shareholders do not get basis for entity-level liabilities, even if they guarantee the debt. The only debt that gives S Corp basis is direct loans made from the shareholder to the corporation. Contrast this clearly on the board to prevent students from carrying partnership liability rules into S Corporation scenarios.

tasks: Determine if an entity meets eligibility criteria for an S corp election.
Calculate shareholder stock basis adjustments based on pass-through items.

sessions.title: Partnerships
sessions.description: Study partnership formations, capital accounts, ordinary business income, and separate pass-through items.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by drawing a sharp conceptual contrast between corporate entities and partnerships. Unlike C Corporations, which act as distinct taxpaying silos, partnerships function as flow-through conduits under Subchapter K. This means the entity itself is a tax-reporting vessel, not a taxpayer, and its economic activities flow directly to the partners' individual returns via Schedule K-1. To ground this visualization, we map out a dual-column ledger on the whiteboard showing the 'Inside Basis' (the partnership's basis in its own assets) and 'Outside Basis' (the partner's basis in their partnership interest). Bridging these two perspectives is critical because students often confuse how transactions at the partnership level echo back to adjust a partner's personal tax footprint.

Next, we transition to partnership formations under Section 721. We illustrate the general rule that no gain or loss is recognized by a partner or the partnership upon a contribution of property in exchange for an interest. This is a crucial concept-first pivot: we must draw a direct comparison back to corporate formations under Section 351, pointing out that unlike Section 351, Section 721 does not impose an 80% control threshold. Anyone can form a partnership at any time tax-free, provided they contribute property. However, we immediately introduce the primary exception to this rule: contributing services instead of property. On the whiteboard, we outline the difference between receiving a capital interest (taxable immediately as ordinary income at fair market value) versus a profits interest (generally non-taxable at formation because the future cash flows are speculative). We walk through a diagnostic scenario where a partner contributes depreciated property with a liability attached, demonstrating how the partner can trigger a taxable gain if the liability assumed by the other partners exceeds the contributing partner's tax basis in the property.

This leads directly to the mechanics of Section 752 debt allocation, which is one of the most high-frequency pitfalls on the CPA Exam. Partners often mistakenly assume that all partnership liabilities increase their basis equally. On the board, we split partnership debt into two paths: Recourse Debt and Nonrecourse Debt. We show that recourse debt is allocated based on who bears the ultimate economic risk of loss, which typically aligns with general partners' capital loss sharing ratios, whereas nonrecourse debt is secured by the property itself and is allocated based on profit-sharing percentages. We write out a step-by-step mathematical derivation of how a new partner's basis is calculated: Adjusted Basis of contributed property, minus the portion of liability shifted to other partners, plus the partner's share of existing partnership liabilities. We walk through an interactive whiteboard exercise where a partner contributes land with a $50,000 basis and a $30,000 mortgage, and the partnership is split 50/50. Working this out dynamically shows how the net effect on their outside basis is a net decrease of $15,000 (representing the 50% liability assumed by the other partner), leaving them with a $35,000 starting basis.

Finally, we tackle the partition of partnership income, mapping out the flow of funds to demonstrate why we must separate ordinary business operations from 'separately stated items.' On the whiteboard, we draw a funnel. At the top of the funnel is the partnership's gross revenue and standard operational expenses, which resolve into Ordinary Business Income or Loss. Separately stated items, such as capital gains, charitable contributions, Section 179 expenses, and dividend income, bypass this primary operational calculation and drop straight through to individual partner tax returns. The teaching point here is deep and structural: these items must be separated because their tax treatment depends entirely on the individual partner's unique tax position (for example, a partner's ability to deduct charitable contributions is subject to individual AGI limits, which the partnership cannot pre-determine). We end the session by visualizing a complete K-1 flow, showing how both ordinary income and separately stated items adjust the partner's outside basis annually, preparing students to confidently tackle both calculation-heavy basis questions and conceptual tax-reporting simulations.

tasks: Calculate partner basis when debt is allocated under Section 752.
Distinguish ordinary partnership income from separately stated items.

sessions.title: Limited Liability Entities
sessions.description: Understand multi-member and single-member LLC structures, default tax classifications, and operational regulations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a fundamental confusion that traps many candidates on the CPA exam: the distinction between a legal entity and its tax classification. On the whiteboard, draw two distinct columns. The first column is labeled 'Legal Form' and the second is labeled 'Tax Treatment.' Under 'Legal Form,' write 'Limited Liability Company (LLC).' Explain that an LLC is purely a creature of state law, designed to provide its owners—known as members—with the same liability shield as corporate shareholders. Under 'Tax Treatment,' draw arrows pointing to three options: Disregarded Entity, Partnership, and Corporation. This visualization immediately drives home the point that the IRS does not recognize an 'LLC' as a federal tax classification on its own; instead, it must fit into one of the existing tax boxes under the federal Check-the-Box regulations.

Next, dive into the mechanics of these default tax classifications using a clear branching diagram. For a single-member LLC, draw an arrow to the default tax status: a 'Disregarded Entity.' Explain that for tax purposes, the entity is ignored, and its activities flow directly onto the owner's individual tax return. For a sole individual owner, this means reporting operations on Schedule C, Schedule E, or Schedule F of Form 1040. For a multi-member LLC, draw an arrow to the default tax status of a 'Partnership,' which requires filing Form 1065 and issuing Schedule K-1s to its members. The core teaching point here is that these classifications happen automatically unless the entity files Form 8832 to elect to be taxed as a C Corporation, or Form 2553 to elect S Corporation status.

Now, pivot to the crucial liability distinction that frequently appears on the exam, contrasting LLC members with general partners. On the whiteboard, sketch a comparison grid. Under 'General Partnership,' illustrate a scenario where the partnership assets are exhausted, showing that creditors can freely cross the boundary to seize the general partner's personal home or bank account due to unlimited joint and several liability. In contrast, under 'LLC,' draw a thick protective wall representing the liability shield. Even if the LLC's assets drop to zero, creditors generally cannot breach this wall to reach the members' personal assets. The members' risk of loss is strictly limited to their capital contribution. This conceptual contrast helps candidates build a solid intuitive foundation for answering operational regulation questions.

Conclude the session with an active learning check to test these concepts. Present a scenario where an individual starts an LLC alone, but later admits a business partner who contributes cash for a 50% interest. Ask the class to track the shift in tax compliance forms and liability status. Students should identify that the entity transitions from filing Schedule C (as a disregarded entity) to filing Form 1065 (as a partnership). Address a common pitfall: remind students that while the tax filing requirements completely change, the underlying legal liability shield remains intact for both owners throughout the transition, protecting them from personal exposure to business debts.

tasks: Identify tax forms used for single-member vs. multi-member LLC structures.
Differentiate LLC member liability from general partner liabilities.

sessions.title: Estates and Trusts
sessions.description: Analyze income tax rules for trusts, fiduciary duties, distributable net income (DNI), and beneficiary distributions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by establishing the unique dual nature of fiduciary entities, which act as both taxable entities and pass-through conduits. On the whiteboard, draw two parallel columns to contrast Fiduciary Accounting Income (FAI) with Taxable Income. Explain that FAI is governed by the trust agreement and local law (Principal and Income Act), determining what belongs to the income beneficiary versus the remainderman, while Taxable Income is governed strictly by the Internal Revenue Code. Introducing this distinction early prevents the most common student error: treating trust accounting distributions and tax deductions as identical concepts. Highlight that a trust is a hybrid entity that gets a deduction for distributions made, shifting the tax burden to the beneficiaries up to a specific limit.

To formalize this limit, we derive the formula for Distributable Net Income (DNI) on the center board. Sketch out the mathematical progression starting from taxable income before the distribution deduction. Show how we add back the personal exemption, add tax-exempt interest (reduced by allocable expenses), and subtract capital gains allocated to the corpus (principal). Emphasize that DNI serves a dual purpose: it limits the distribution deduction allowable to the estate or trust, and it characterizes the income received by the beneficiaries. Walk through why capital gains are typically excluded from DNI—because they are usually reinvested in the corpus for the remainderman rather than distributed to current income beneficiaries. Address the trap of forgetting to reduce tax-exempt interest by its share of trustee fees, which is a high-frequency exam pitfall.

Next, draw a clear classification matrix to differentiate Simple Trusts from Complex Trusts. Illustrate that a Simple Trust must distribute all of its income currently, cannot distribute principal, and cannot make charitable contributions, receiving a standard annual exemption of $300. In contrast, show how a Complex Trust may accumulate income, distribute principal, or make charitable contributions, receiving an exemption of $100. Use a flowchart to map how a trust can shift from simple to complex in any given tax year based on actual distributions made, reinforcing that classification is an annual operational determination rather than just a boilerplate legal designation.

Conclude the session with a practical whiteboard application scenario. Present a complex trust with $50,000 in dividends, $20,000 in tax-exempt interest, $10,000 in capital gains allocated to corpus, and $5,000 in trustee fees. Guide the students through calculating FAI, DNI, and the trust's taxable income under different distribution scenarios (e.g., distributing $30,000 versus distributing $60,000). This interactive derivation demonstrates how the distribution deduction is capped at the lesser of actual distributions or DNI (adjusted for tax-exempt items), solidifying their mechanical and conceptual mastery of fiduciary taxation.

tasks: Calculate distributable net income (DNI) for a complex trust.
Identify differences between simple and complex trust classifications.

sessions.title: Tax-Exempt Organizations
sessions.description: Examine qualification criteria for Section 501(c)(3) status, annual reporting (Form 990), and unrelated business income tax (UBIT).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by defining the core architecture of tax-exempt status, specifically focusing on Internal Revenue Code Section 501(c)(3). In a public lecture style, we set up a visual taxonomy on the board, splitting the eligibility requirements into three pillars: organizational purpose (such as religious, charitable, scientific, or educational), the absolute prohibition against private inurement (where net earnings cannot benefit private shareholders or individuals), and the strict limitation on political campaigning and substantial lobbying. This sets a strong conceptual foundation, helping students grasp that tax-exempt status is a granted privilege tied to public benefit rather than a natural right of corporate existence.

Next, we transition the board to analyze annual compliance and reporting mechanisms under IRS Form 990. Because the CPA Exam frequently tests the exceptions to the filing requirement, we outline a clear mnemonic and category tree. We visually isolate the specific entities exempt from filing this annual informational return, grouping them into religious organizations (churches, missionary societies), certain state institutions, and very small organizations below the standard gross receipts thresholds. By explaining why these specific carve-outs exist (mainly due to constitutional protections regarding religion and administrative convenience), students can intuitively predict which entities are exempt rather than attempting rote memorization.

We then address the critical, high-frequency exam concept of Unrelated Business Income Tax (UBIT). On the whiteboard, we map out the logical chain that triggers UBIT. This requires three concurrent tests: the activity must be a trade or business, it must be regularly carried on, and it must not be substantially related to the organization's tax-exempt purpose. To solidify this concept, we walk through a classic diagnostic scenario on the board—contrasting a university bookstore selling textbooks (related/exempt) versus that same bookstore operating a commercial travel agency or a public parking lot on weekdays (unrelated/taxable). We specifically highlight a common pitfall: students often mistakenly assume that because the *profits* of the business are fully dedicated to the charity's mission, the income itself becomes tax-exempt. We visually debunk this myth on the board, demonstrating that taxation is determined by the *source* of the income, not the *destination* of the funds.

To close the session, we conduct a structured whiteboard calculation of Net Unrelated Business Income (UBI). We write out the computational formula, showing how gross income from the unrelated trade or business is offset by directly connected business deductions, subject to specific statutory exclusions like dividends, interest, royalties, rents from real property (unless debt-financed), and a standard $1,000 specific deduction. This step-by-step mathematical breakdown equips students with the exact framework needed to isolate taxable UBI from exempt passive income streams, reinforcing both the definitions and the application mechanics required for the CPA Exam.

tasks: Calculate taxable unrelated business income (UBI) for an exempt entity.
Identify organizations exempt from filing the annual Form 990.

projects.stage_description: Calculate individual taxable income and corporate taxable income for a shareholder and their C Corporation, identifying opportunities for legal tax avoidance under current IRS tax code regulations.
