units.title: Business Analysis and Reporting — BAR Discipline
units.description: Deep dive into financial statement analysis, ratio evaluations, cost classifications, risk management structures, and complex accounting transactions.

lectures.title: Business Analysis
lectures.description: Covers financial analysis methods, data representation, projection models, and standard business valuation techniques.

sessions.title: Financial Statement Analysis
sessions.description: Apply horizontal, vertical, and trend analysis methods to analyze balance sheets and income statements.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing candidates to the fundamental philosophy of financial statement analysis. In the CPA exam context, raw numbers on a balance sheet or income statement are rarely sufficient on their own; we must convert them into relational and temporal metrics to extract meaningful strategic insights. The teacher should start on the whiteboard by drawing a simple contrast between absolute dollar increases and proportional changes. This sets up the conceptual framework: why do we need vertical and horizontal analysis? The core message here is scale-independence. By converting financial statements into common-size formats or trend percentages, we can compare a multinational conglomerate with a mid-sized regional competitor, or track a single firm's efficiency over multiple volatile market cycles.

Next, the whiteboard transition turns to Vertical Analysis, also known as creating common-size financial statements. The teacher should visually construct a comparative income statement and a comparative balance sheet side-by-side. The critical concept to emphasize is the 'anchor base.' On the income statement, every single line item—from cost of goods sold to net income—is expressed as a percentage of Net Sales or Revenue (the 100% anchor). On the balance sheet, the anchor shifts to Total Assets (or, equivalently, Total Liabilities and Shareholders' Equity). A frequent student pitfall is choosing the wrong base, such as using Gross Profit instead of Net Sales when analyzing operating expenses, which distorts the vertical percentage. The teacher should explicitly write down these formulas and map out a visual flow showing how cash, inventory, and equipment scale relative to total assets, explaining how this reveals shifts in asset intensity or capitalization strategies.

Following vertical analysis, the lesson shifts to Horizontal Analysis and Trend Analysis, which evaluate performance over time rather than within a single period. The teacher will write out the classic formula for percentage change: (Current Year Value minus Base Year Value) divided by Base Year Value. To build true intuition, the teacher should draw a multi-year timeline representing operational revenue over four consecutive years. Here, the instructor must address a high-frequency exam pitfall: the mathematical trap of calculating percentage changes when the base year is zero or negative (such as moving from a net loss to a net profit). The teacher should explain how to handle these anomalies in professional practice, reminding students that percentage changes lose logical meaning in such scenarios, and alternative qualitative or absolute metrics must be highlighted instead.

To solidify these concepts, the teacher will lead a guided whiteboard practice scenario. The scenario features a comparative income statement of a retail startup experiencing rapid revenue growth but unexpected net losses. The teacher will write out two years of numbers: Year 1 and Year 2 revenue, cost of goods sold, and operating expenses. First, the teacher will prompt students to calculate the year-over-year percentage trend for operational revenue, illustrating a massive top-line expansion. Second, the teacher will perform a vertical analysis of both years' operating expenses. This vertical analysis will reveal the hidden culprit: while revenue grew by fifty percent, SG&A expenses as a percentage of sales ballooned from fifteen percent to thirty percent. This interactive walkthrough demonstrates to students how combining horizontal and vertical tools uncovers operational inefficiencies that absolute dollar values obscure, preparing them directly for complex task-based simulations on the BAR discipline exam.

tasks: Perform vertical analysis on a comparative income statement.
Calculate year-over-year percentage trends for operational revenue.

sessions.title: Financial Ratios
sessions.description: Calculate and interpret liquidity, solvency, leverage, profitability, and asset efficiency ratios.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to our whiteboard session on Financial Ratios, a critical component of the BAR discipline on the CPA Exam. Our learner profile requests a concept-first, public lecture style. Rather than forcing memorization of a massive ratio matrix, we will construct these formulas using a visual balance sheet architecture, focusing on the underlying economic reality that each metric captures. We will start by drawing a simplified, high-level balance sheet on the whiteboard, separating assets into current and non-current, and liabilities into short-term obligations and long-term capital. This visual anchor prevents a common candidate pitfall: blindly pulling numbers without verifying if they fit the liquidity or solvency definition. Let's establish that liquidity measures immediate survival, while solvency and leverage assess long-term viability and structural risk.

We will begin our interactive whiteboard build by mapping out the liquidity spectrum, progressing from the most inclusive to the most conservative metric. Draw three concentric circles representing the assets available to meet short-term obligations. The largest circle represents Current Assets (current ratio), the middle represents Quick Assets (quick ratio, which strips out inventory and prepaid expenses due to their lower conversion speed), and the innermost circle represents Cash and Cash Equivalents (cash ratio). We will explain the rationale behind these adjustments, highlighting how inventory valuation or obsolescence can artificially inflate a standard current ratio. We will then walk through a scenario: a retailer holds significant inventory that is difficult to liquidate quickly. This scenario perfectly demonstrates why their current ratio looks healthy at 2.0, while their quick ratio reveals a hazardous liquidity squeeze at 0.5. By deriving these formulas visually, candidates learn to analyze the quality of working capital rather than just calculating a math formula.

Next, we transition from short-term liquidity to long-term leverage and solvency. On the whiteboard, we will draw a balance scale. On one side, we place Total Debt (both short and long-term interest-bearing liabilities); on the other, we place Total Equity. We will walk through the Debt-to-Equity and Debt-to-Assets formulas, demonstrating how leverage acts as a double-edged sword that amplifies returns during upswings but increases default risk during downturns. To bridge this into profitability and asset efficiency, we will introduce the concept of asset turnover and inventory turnover. We will write out the inventory turnover formula, emphasizing that Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) from the income statement must be paired with *Average* Inventory from the balance sheet. This mismatch between flow variables (income statement) and point-in-time variables (balance sheet) is a frequent source of exam errors; we will emphasize the logical necessity of using average balances to maintain statistical integrity.

To consolidate these concepts, we will walk through a guided practice problem using raw financial data drawn on the whiteboard. We will present a comparative balance sheet and an income statement for a manufacturing company. First, we will ask the class to calculate the current, quick, and cash ratios. This exercise is designed to reveal if candidates can quickly filter out irrelevant line items (such as equipment or accounts payable) and identify the core components of the liquid asset pool. Second, we will have them evaluate the firm's operational efficiency by calculating the inventory turnover ratio and converting it into days sales in inventory. We will conclude the session by demonstrating how to interpret these results together: a high inventory turnover combined with a low quick ratio might indicate that a firm is operating dangerously close to stockouts, linking operational efficiency directly back to liquidity risk.

tasks: Calculate current, quick, and cash ratios from balance sheet data.
Evaluate a firm's operational efficiency using inventory turnover ratios.

sessions.title: Data Analysis and Visualization
sessions.description: Identify structures for analyzing business data, using visualization plots, and extracting insights from database tables.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing a concept-first foundation for data structure and classification in business analytics. Before students dive into technical database architectures or complex charts, they must first master how to categorize business data into structured, semi-structured, and unstructured formats, and recognize qualitative versus quantitative variables. The teacher will draw a simple taxonomy on the board, demonstrating how transaction records in a general ledger represent structured data with defined fields, whereas unstructured data might include customer feedback emails or invoice images. The key objective here is to help candidates develop an intuitive diagnostic habit: looking at any business data source and instantly identifying its structural properties, which dictates how that data can be queried and visualized.

Transitioning from classification to visualization, we will illustrate the core principles of selecting the right graphical representation based on analytical objectives. Instead of memorizing chart types mechanically, students will explore a visual decision tree on the whiteboard. The teacher will outline scenarios where line charts are critical for showcasing trends over time (such as sales trajectory over successive quarters) and contrast them with bar charts for categorical comparisons, scatter plots for identifying correlations, and histograms for frequency distributions. We will directly address a common CPA pitfall here: candidates frequently confuse histogram distribution patterns with line-chart time trends. By sketching both side-by-side, the teacher will show how time is an independent variable sequencing left-to-right, whereas a histogram aggregates frequency counts regardless of chronological order.

Next, we introduce basic database structures and querying logic, specifically focusing on how relational databases store ledger transactions. The teacher will draw two simplified tables on the whiteboard: a 'Sales_Transactions' table and a 'Customer_Master' table. Rather than writing raw, complex SQL, the focus is on understanding logical joins and field extractions. We will walk through how a 'Customer_ID' acts as a primary key in one table and a foreign key in another to link transaction amounts to specific customer demographics. The core teaching point here is to demystify how structured query outputs are generated and how an analyst translates a business question (such as 'which region has the highest transaction frequency?') into a data extraction workflow.

To cement these concepts, the session concludes with a structured practice walkthrough. The teacher will present a sample mock database table showing five transaction entries alongside three different chart draft options. Students will be asked to identify which chart correctly represents the trend over time and spot anomalies in a simulated database query output, such as duplicated transaction rows due to a faulty join. This exercise is specifically designed to uncover whether students can spot inconsistencies between raw tabular ledger data and its visual representation, building the diagnostic eye required for data integrity questions on the CPA exam.

tasks: Select the appropriate chart type to represent trends over time.
Interpret database output queries related to sales ledger transactions.

sessions.title: Forecasting and Projection
sessions.description: Apply regression analysis and regression outputs to project future revenue and operating costs.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by framing forecasting not as guesswork, but as a systematic statistical discipline. In the BAR section of the CPA exam, candidates must transition from simple historical averages to multi-variable quantitative models. Introduce the core linear regression equation, expressing it on the whiteboard as Y equals a plus bX, or in managerial terms, Total Cost equals Fixed Costs plus Variable Cost per unit times volume. It is crucial to define Y as the dependent variable—the outcome we wish to predict, such as operating costs or revenue—and X as the independent variable, which is the operational driver. Explain that establishing this mathematical relationship allows organizations to defend their budgets and projections with statistical rigor rather than subjective intuition.

To build visual intuition, draw a scatter plot on the whiteboard with historical cost data points scattered across activity levels. Illustrate how the ordinary least squares regression line cuts through these points, explaining that the algorithm mathematically minimizes the sum of the squared vertical distances between the actual data points and the regression line itself. Point out the vertical intercept on the Y-axis as the fixed cost component, and the slope of the line as the variable rate. At this moment, warn students about the high-frequency pitfall of ignoring the 'relevant range'. A regression line is only valid within the boundaries of the historical activity levels observed; projecting costs at zero volume or double the current capacity using the same equation violates fundamental cost-behavior assumptions and leads to invalid projections.

Next, transition to interpreting computer-generated regression logs, which is a highly tested task-based simulation scenario. Draw a simplified regression output table on the whiteboard, highlighting three critical metrics: the Coefficient of Determination (R-squared), the t-statistic, and the p-value. Explain that R-squared measures the goodness of fit—specifically, the percentage of variation in the dependent variable explained by the independent variable. Distinguish this from the correlation coefficient (r) to prevent confusion. Then, explain that the p-value indicates whether the relationship observed is statistically significant or merely a product of random chance. Teach students to look for a p-value of less than 0.05 as the standard threshold for statistical significance, meaning we are 95% confident the driver actually influences the cost.

Incorporate an interactive diagnostic checkpoint on the whiteboard. Present students with a mock regression log for utility costs where the R-squared is a high 0.88, but the p-value for 'average outdoor temperature' is 0.22. Guide them to recognize that despite the high overall R-squared, temperature is not a statistically significant driver in this model, and relying on it for projections would be a major operational error. This exercise is designed to reveal whether students are blindly looking at overall fit metrics without validating individual variable strength, which is a classic distractor on multiple-choice questions.

Conclude the session with a hands-on projection application. Write down a derived regression formula on the whiteboard for a company's distribution expenses: Y equals $125,000 plus $8.50 per shipment. Walk through the calculation step-by-step to project expenses for an upcoming quarter where shipments are expected to reach 15,000 units. Solve for Y, obtaining $252,500. Show how to audit this result by breaking it back down into its fixed base and variable component. Emphasize that in simulation tasks, candidates might be asked to adjust this baseline projection for known future changes, such as a 5% inflation increase on the fixed cost component, demonstrating how mathematical outputs must always be integrated with practical business realities.

tasks: Project corporate expenses using a linear regression formula.
Analyze statistical significance variables in computer-generated regression logs.

sessions.title: Business Valuation
sessions.description: Understand valuation models: discounted cash flow (DCF), market multiples, and asset-based approaches.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing the core premise of business valuation: determining what a business is worth by looking at its future cash generation, its comparable peers, and its underlying assets. Since the learner preferred a concept-first, public-lecture style, we start with a highly intuitive, conceptual framing. We write three pillars on the whiteboard: 'The Income Approach (Future Cash Flow)', 'The Market Approach (Relative Pricing)', and 'The Asset Approach (Liquidation/Cost Value)'. We explain that valuation is not a single calculation but a mosaic of these three perspectives. We address a common misconception early: many students mistakenly assume a company's balance sheet equity represents its market value. We visually contrast the accounting book value of assets with the economic value of future cash flows to show why market values diverged from historical costs.

Next, we dive deep into the first pillar: the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model. To make this derivation intuitive, we draw a timeline of explicit forecast years followed by a terminal value horizon. We write out the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) equation and show how it acts as the discount rate reflecting risk. Step-by-step, we derive the Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF) formula on the board, tracing how we adjust operating income (EBIT) by adding back non-cash expenses like depreciation, and subtracting capital expenditures and changes in working capital. We intentionally highlight a classic exam pitfall: forgetting to tax-shield EBIT or incorrectly using net income instead of operating income. Once the explicit period is established, we introduce the Gordon Growth Method for Terminal Value. We write the formula TV = [FCF_n * (1 + g)] / (WACC - g) and graphically show how a small change in the perpetual growth rate (g) dramatically swings the terminal value, teaching students to treat this assumption with caution.

We then transition to our first practice exercise: calculating enterprise value using a multi-period DCF model with terminal growth. Instead of just showing the math, we walk through the workflow as a narrative. We have students discount each explicit cash flow, calculate the terminal value at the end of year five, discount that terminal value back to Year 0, and sum them to arrive at the Enterprise Value. This practice reveals whether students understand the time value of money mechanics and the massive weight that terminal value holds in a typical valuation.

From the absolute value of the DCF, we pivot to relative valuation: Market Multiples. We explain that while DCF is theoretically robust, market multiples provide a sanity check based on actual transaction data. We write down key multiples, focusing on Enterprise Value to EBITDA (EV/EBITDA). We draw a clear distinction between enterprise-level multiples (which use EV and measure the value of the entire operating business to all capital providers) and equity-level multiples (like P/E, which look only at shareholders). We warn students about the logical error of pairing an enterprise metric with an equity metric (e.g., EV/Net Income). We show how to strip away debt from EV to arrive at Equity Value, and then divide by outstanding shares to estimate share price.

To solidify this, we run our second practice task: estimating share price values using EV/EBITDA multiples. We present a scenario where a target company has a known EBITDA, and we observe peer multiples. We guide students to apply the average peer multiple to calculate target EV, subtract net debt, and divide by shares outstanding. This exercise shows students how capital structure adjustments directly impact the estimated per-share value.

We close the session by briefly contrasting these two dynamic approaches with the Asset-Based Approach, which acts as a floor value for asset-heavy or liquidating firms. We summarize by showing how a professional valuation report compares these methods in a 'football field' chart on the whiteboard, demonstrating that the best valuation is a synthesis of rigorous DCF derivation and realistic market multiples. This structural workflow equips candidates to tackle both complex calculation questions and conceptual evaluation tasks on the CPA Exam.

tasks: Calculate enterprise value using a discounted cash flow formula with terminal growth.
Estimate share price values using enterprise value/EBITDA multiples.

lectures.title: Planning and Performance Management
lectures.description: Covers cost systems, budget modeling, variance investigations, and working capital optimization policies.

sessions.title: Budgeting and Planning
sessions.description: Construct operational budgets, master budgets, cash budgets, and flexible budget adjustments.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by introducing the master budget as an integrated network of operating and financial decisions, rather than a collection of isolated spreadsheets. Our goal is to establish a concept-first, highly visual 'whiteboard' layout that displays how sales forecasts drive the entire production plan, which then splits into direct materials, direct labor, and overhead requirements. This flow is critical because candidates often struggle to see how a small change in forecasted sales ripple through the cash disbursements. I will draw a flow diagram on the board starting with the Sales Budget at the top, cascading down into the Production Budget, and ultimately converging into the Cash Budget. This shows students that budgeting is a logical chain where every output serves as an input for the next phase.

Next, we transition to constructing a detailed corporate quarterly cash budget, focusing heavily on cash collections and disbursements. When illustrating cash collections, I will map out how sales from prior quarters affect current quarter inflows based on credit collection percentages. This is where most students trip up: they mix up cash collections with accrual revenue. I will write a simple timeline on the board showing a $100,000 credit sale in January and tracing its collection across February and March to visually separate the accounting timing from the actual liquidity. We will then perform a step-by-step assembly of cash outflows, highlighting how raw material purchases, payroll, and fixed overhead payments are timed, ensuring we distinguish non-cash expenses like depreciation from actual cash outflows.

Once the cash receipts and disbursements are mapped, we will address short-term financing and cash policy buffers. I will draw a horizontal line on the board representing the 'Minimum Cash Balance Requirement.' We will simulate a scenario where the ending cash balance drops below this line, forcing the business to draw from a line of credit, and conversely, a scenario where excess cash is generated and used to pay down outstanding principal or interest. This helps the learner see the cash budget not just as a static forecast, but as a dynamic management tool for maintaining corporate liquidity.

To bridge the master budget to performance evaluation, we will dive into the mechanics of flexible budgeting. I will write down a static budget designed for 10,000 units side-by-side with actual results for 12,000 units. By demonstrating how unfair and misleading it is to evaluate manager performance using a static model when volume changes, I will introduce the concept of 'flexing' the budget. On the whiteboard, we will isolate variable costs and adjust them using a unit-based formula (Budgeted Variable Cost per Unit multiplied by Actual Units produced), while keeping budgeted fixed costs constant. This ensures students understand that a flexible budget is the ultimate tool for a true 'apples-to-apples' variance comparison.

We will wrap up the session with an interactive practice run where we adapt a static budget to actual output levels on the fly. I will write down the initial static assumptions, prompt the class to identify which costs are truly variable versus fixed, and run the calculations to build the flexed budget. Throughout this walkthrough, I will explicitly highlight common exam pitfalls, such as mistakenly scaling fixed costs in proportion to volume increases, and reinforce the underlying structural behavior of both cost types.

tasks: Prepare a detailed corporate cash budget for a quarterly period.
Adapt static budgets to actual output levels using flexible budgeting formulas.

sessions.title: Cost Accounting
sessions.description: Differentiate job costing, process costing, activity-based costing (ABC), and joint product allocations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing the foundational architecture of product costing. The main objective is to help students visually map out how costs flow from raw materials through work-in-process to finished goods under different manufacturing environments. To hook the learners, we present a stark contrast: a custom luxury yacht builder versus a high-volume soft drink bottling plant. This naturally sets up the conceptual separation between Job Costing, where unique overhead batches are tracked via individual jobs, and Process Costing, where homogenous units flow continuously. On our whiteboard, we will sketch a parallel workflow path. This initial framing is vital because it prevents students from treating cost accounting as a set of disconnected formulas; instead, they see that the physical nature of production dictates the accounting architecture.

Next, we transition to the core technical hurdle of Process Costing: Equivalent Units of Production (EUP). This concept often confuses candidates because it demands that we quantify partially completed products in terms of fully completed units. On the whiteboard, draw a container representing Work-in-Process (WIP) that is 40% complete. We will explicitly derive the mathematical difference between the Weighted-Average and FIFO methods. Under Weighted-Average, we blend prior period costs and work with current period costs, ignoring the timing of when the work was started. Under FIFO, we strictly segregate beginning inventory work from current period work. We will write out the step-by-step physical flow and equivalent units calculation on the board, demonstrating that FIFO only counts work actually performed in the current period. A common pitfall here is when students mistakenly include the work already done on beginning inventory during the prior period in their FIFO calculations. To counter this, we will use a visual timeline to prove that FIFO EUP equals (Beginning WIP % to complete) + (Units Started & Completed) + (Ending WIP % completed).

Following this derivation, we introduce an interactive classroom practice challenge. We will ask students to calculate EUP for a business with 1,000 units in beginning WIP (60% complete), 5,000 units started, and 800 units in ending WIP (25% complete) under both methods. Working through this live on the board allows the teacher to highlight the classic trap: how materials added at the very beginning of a process vs. materials added conversion-style throughout the process impact equivalent units. This exercise is designed to reveal whether students can separate the timing of direct material additions from the gradual application of conversion costs.

With the foundation of volume-based costing established, we pivot to Activity-Based Costing (ABC) to address the limitations of traditional overhead allocation. Traditional costing often distorts product margins by allocating overhead using a single, plant-wide volume driver like direct labor hours. On the whiteboard, we will construct a comparative scenario of two products: one high-volume and simple, the other low-volume and highly customized. By illustrating how a single overhead rate overcosts high-volume products and undercosts low-volume, complex products, we demonstrate the necessity of ABC. We will draw a flow diagram showing how overhead resources are first assigned to activity cost pools (such as machine setups, quality inspections, and material handling) and then allocated to products using specific activity drivers. We will walk through the algebraic step of calculating individual activity rates and applying them, reinforcing that ABC provides a more accurate cost representation for strategic pricing decisions.

Finally, we will address Joint Product Costing and the byproduct dilemma. When a single manufacturing input yields multiple distinct outputs at a 'split-off point', standard costing rules apply. We will draw a branching tree diagram on the board to illustrate this split-off point, distinguishing between joint products and byproducts. We will mathematically demonstrate the Physical Measure Method versus the Net Realizable Value (NRV) Method for allocating joint costs. The key takeaway for candidates here is understanding that joint costs incurred before the split-off point are sunk and irrelevant to the decision of whether to sell a product at split-off or process it further. We wrap up by showing how byproducts are accounted for, either as a reduction of joint costs or as miscellaneous revenue, leaving students with a clear, visual map of the entire cost accounting landscape.

tasks: Calculate equivalent units of production under FIFO and weighted average process costing.
Allocate manufacturing overhead pools using activity-based cost drivers.

sessions.title: Variance Analysis
sessions.description: Analyze variances for direct materials, direct labor, and overhead spending/efficiency.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing the conceptual philosophy behind standard costing and variance analysis. The core idea is that variance analysis is not just a calculation exercise, but a diagnostic tool to evaluate operational efficiency and price control. On the whiteboard, we will draw three main columns to represent the standard cost flow: Actual Cost (Actual Quantity x Actual Price), the Split/Hybrid point (Actual Quantity x Standard Price), and Standard Cost (Standard Quantity Allowed x Standard Price). This visual framework, often referred to as the 'AQ*AP vs AQ*SP vs SQ*SP' model, serves as the absolute backbone for isolating price-related and quantity-related discrepancies. By first visualizing how these columns interact, learners can intuitively understand that by holding price constant (using standard price in the middle and right columns), we isolate quantity differences, and by holding quantity constant (using actual quantity in the left and middle columns), we isolate price differences.

Next, we transition directly into the mechanics of Direct Materials (DM) variances. The primary pitfall for candidates on the CPA Exam is misidentifying the point of purchase versus the point of usage. We will whiteboard a concrete scenario where a manufacturing firm purchases a different amount of raw materials than what they actually put into production. The instructor must highlight that the Direct Materials Price Variance is calculated at the point of purchase using the Quantity Purchased, because this is when the purchasing manager exerts control over the price. Conversely, the Direct Materials Quantity (or Usage) Variance must be calculated using the Quantity Used in production, to isolate the efficiency of the production manager. On the board, write out the explicit derivations of both formulas and demonstrate how the split columns handle this dual-quantity issue without creating math errors.

Following the materials segment, we apply the exact same three-column logical framework to Direct Labor (DL) variances. Here, we transition terminology from 'price' and 'quantity' to 'rate' and 'efficiency'. We will show that the Direct Labor Rate Variance reflects the difference between what we paid our workforce per hour and what we planned to pay, while the Labor Efficiency Variance measures how many hours our workforce actually took compared to the standard hours allowed for the actual output achieved. We will address a high-frequency exam pitfall: the economic trade-off. For example, if a company hires highly skilled (and therefore more expensive) labor, this leads to an unfavorable labor rate variance but a highly favorable labor efficiency variance because they work faster with fewer errors. Drawing these balance-of-tradeoffs on the board prevents rote memorization and fosters true business intuition.

To solidify these concepts, we will walk through a live practice scenario on the whiteboard. We will provide a standard card for a single product requiring 2 pounds of material at $5/pound and 1.5 hours of labor at $20/hour. Then, provide the actual quarterly production data (e.g., 5,000 units produced, 11,000 pounds purchased at $4.80/pound, 10,200 pounds used in production, and 7,200 actual labor hours at $20.50/hour). Step-by-step, the instructor will guide students to calculate the Direct Materials Price Variance, DM Quantity Variance, DL Rate Variance, and DL Efficiency Variance. We will highlight the common calculation mistake of calculating 'Standard Quantity' using the budgeted production units instead of the actual units achieved. This practice exercise acts as a diagnostic diagnostic, forcing learners to reconcile actual activity levels against standard expectations before proceeding.

tasks: Calculate direct materials price and quantity variances.
Isolate labor rate and efficiency variances from operational reports.

sessions.title: Performance Measures
sessions.description: Evaluate divisional profit structures using return on investment (ROI), residual income (RI), and the Balanced Scorecard framework.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard-driven session by framing the fundamental tension in divisional performance measurement: how to evaluate a segment manager's success without creating incentives that harm the parent corporation. First, we establish the conceptual foundations of Return on Investment (ROI). I will draw a basic formula on the board showing ROI as Operating Income divided by Average Operating Assets. By decomposing this using the DuPont model into Profit Margin (Operating Income / Sales) and Asset Turnover (Sales / Average Operating Assets), we visualize for students how a division can improve its return either by boosting profitability per dollar of sales or by spinning its assets faster. This conceptual-first breakdown is crucial because students often fail to see that ROI is not just a single static ratio, but a dynamic interplay of operational efficiency and asset management.

Next, we introduce the major strategic flaw of ROI: the suboptimization trap. To demonstrate this on the whiteboard, I will walk through a concrete scenario where a division manager with a current high ROI of 20% rejects a new, highly profitable project yielding 15% because it would drag down their divisional average. I will draw a parallel timeline of events showing how this decision benefits the manager's bonus but hurts the overall corporation whose cost of capital is only 10%. This leads naturally to the introduction of Residual Income (RI) as the mathematical antidote. I will write the formula on the board: Residual Income = Operating Income - (Average Operating Assets x Required Rate of Return). By calculating RI for the same scenario, students will visually witness how the project yields a positive dollar-value surplus, aligning the manager's incentives perfectly with corporate goals. This comparison helps clear up the common pitfall where students confuse percentage-based metrics (ROI) with absolute dollar-based metrics (RI), highlighting that while ROI makes comparing divisions of different sizes easier, RI is superior for goal congruence.

We then transition to the Balanced Scorecard framework to address the limitation of relying solely on lagging financial indicators like ROI and RI. I will sketch a four-quadrant matrix on the whiteboard, labeling the perspectives: Financial, Customer, Internal Business Processes, and Learning and Growth. Rather than presenting this as a dry classification list, I will draw cause-and-effect arrows connecting the quadrants. I will illustrate how investing in employee training (Learning and Growth) leads to improved cycle times (Internal Processes), which boosts customer satisfaction and retention (Customer), ultimately driving superior profit margins and higher ROI (Financial). This visual flowchart helps students understand that the Balanced Scorecard is a cohesive strategy map rather than a random collection of operational KPIs.

Finally, we will engage in a diagnostic practice exercise. I will write raw operating data on the board for a hypothetical retail division and ask the class to compute both ROI and RI under different hurdle rates. During this activity, I will monitor for the frequent mistake of including non-operating assets or historical cost valuations that distort the denominator. We will conclude by classifying specific performance metrics—such as customer survey scores, setup times, and employee turnover rates—into their correct scorecard quadrants, reinforcing how financial and non-financial measures work in tandem to evaluate long-term divisional health.

tasks: Calculate and compare return on investment (ROI) against residual income (RI) for a segment.
Classify performance indicators into the four Balanced Scorecard perspectives.

sessions.title: Working Capital Management
sessions.description: Master the cash conversion cycle, factoring, receivables collection terms, and inventory replenishment models (EOQ).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by visualizing the firm's operational cash flow using a horizontal timeline on the whiteboard. This visual representation allows us to conceptualize the complete Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC). The main goal is to show how cash is tied up in operating assets from the moment we purchase raw materials on credit to the day we finally collect cash from our customers, offset by the credit terms our suppliers grant us. Rather than presenting the formula immediately, we draw out the individual timelines for Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO), Days Sales Outstanding (DSO), and Days Payable Outstanding (DPO). The core concept here is that a lower CCC represents a leaner, more liquid organization, while a ballooning CCC signals impending cash flow crises. 

We transition into a step-by-step derivation of each sub-metric, clarifying the underlying logic that connects standard balance sheet metrics to the operating cycle. For DIO, we explain how inventory must be supported by Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), whereas DSO is supported by credit sales. A common point of confusion for students is using total revenue as the denominator for DSO instead of credit sales, or mixing up COGS with sales revenue when calculating DIO. We construct a real-world scenario on the board where a wholesale distributor has $1,000,000 in credit sales and $600,000 in COGS. We calculate the average accounts receivable and inventory balances, and show how to derive the metrics on a 365-day basis. We highlight that DPO is an intentional delay mechanism, acting as a free source of short-term financing, but caution that delaying payables too long can damage supplier relationships and destroy creditworthiness.

Next, we introduce the tactical lever of discount collection policies, such as changing terms from 'net 30' to '2/10, net 30'. On the whiteboard, we map out the quantitative trade-off: a company gives up a small percentage of its top-line revenue to accelerate cash inflows, which in turn reduces its DSO and decreases its borrowing costs or frees up capital for higher-yielding investments. We guide the teacher to run through a quick practice exercise comparing the cost of giving up the discount to the opportunity cost of capital. We show how a 2% discount for cash payment 20 days early equates to an annualized interest rate of over 36%, proving why customers are highly incentivized to take it and how the selling firm must balance this cost against the benefits of reduced carrying costs and lower credit risk.

We then shift our focus to inventory replenishment mechanics through the lens of the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) model. Rather than just handing out the formula, we use the whiteboard to graph the trade-off curves: the downward-sloping ordering cost curve versus the upward-sloping carrying cost curve. The minimum point of the total cost curve is mathematically derived where these two curves intersect. We warn students about a frequent pitfall on the CPA exam: mismatching units. Carrying costs must be expressed per unit per year, and demand must also be annualized. If the problem states weekly demand or monthly storage costs, we must explicitly demonstrate how to convert them before plugging them into the radical sign of the EOQ equation.

Finally, we cover alternative short-term financing strategies, specifically factoring accounts receivable. We map out the difference between factoring with recourse versus factoring without recourse, drawing flow lines to indicate which party bears the ultimate risk of bad debts. This visual distinction helps students understand why factoring without recourse carries a much higher service fee. We close the session with a synthesis practice problem: a firm is experiencing rapid growth, has cash trapped in receivables, and must decide whether to factor its invoices, offer a cash discount, or squeeze its suppliers by extending DPO. By evaluating these options side-by-side on the board, students learn to view working capital not as isolated formulas, but as a dynamic system of lever controls.

tasks: Calculate the cash conversion cycle from days inventory, receivables, and payables outstanding.
Evaluate the cash savings of a discount collection policy change.

sessions.title: Financial Risk Management
sessions.description: Examine techniques to manage interest rate, currency, credit, and operational risks.
sessions.sessionOutline:
This whiteboard session is designed to demystify financial risk management, shifting the learner's focus from dry definitions to a highly visual, conceptual framework that aligns with a public-lecture delivery style. We begin by drawing a clean taxonomy on the board, splitting risk into four primary quadrants: interest rate risk, currency risk, credit risk, and operational risk. Rather than treating these as separate checklists, we visually diagram them as external forces acting upon a firm's balance sheet. We establish why understanding these forces is critical for corporate decision-makers, specifically pointing out how fluctuating macro elements directly impact profitability, debt servicing costs, and cross-border cash flows.

Next, we transition to the mechanics of currency risk, using a clear visual scenario of a US-based firm that has a pending net payable in Euros. On the left side of the whiteboard, we write out the initial exchange rate and the payable amount. On the right, we show a hypothetical depreciation of the US Dollar (and appreciation of the Euro) prior to the settlement date. We lead students through the math of calculating the precise financial impact of this exchange rate shift on net payables, demonstrating how an unhedged position translates directly into an exchange loss on the income statement. A common pitfall here is misidentifying which currency's appreciation hurts the payer; we visual-code the arrows to show that a strengthening foreign currency increases the domestic cash outflow needed to settle the debt.

We then build a bridge from currency volatility to interest rate risk. To visualize this, we draw a timeline of variable-rate debt obligations alongside a swap-clearing diagram. We introduce the concept of interest rate swaps as a mutual agreement to exchange cash flow streams, transforming a volatile floating-rate liability into a predictable fixed-rate commitment. We visually diagram the flows of the swap: the company pays a fixed rate to a financial counterparty and receives a floating rate, which perfectly offsets the floating rate they owe to their primary lenders. This visualizes 'hedging' not as speculative trading, but as an insurance mechanism that locks in cash flow predictability.

To wrap up, we present a brief, interactive classroom check. We prompt students to analyze a scenario where a firm expects to receive foreign currency in ninety days and ask them to determine whether they should buy a forward contract to sell or buy that currency. We sketch out the decision tree on the board, helping them trace the logical chain that a receivable requires selling the foreign currency to lock in the domestic value. This diagnostic exercise ensures students can apply risk-mitigation logic intuitively before they face formal exam-style questions.

tasks: Calculate the impact of a foreign exchange shift on net payables.
Identify strategies to hedge interest rate risk using swap options.

lectures.title: Advanced Financial Reporting
lectures.description: Addresses advanced accounting areas, covering hedges, business acquisitions, public company disclosures, and governmental reconciliations.

sessions.title: Advanced Revenue Recognition
sessions.description: Identify treatments for multiple-element arrangements, bill-and-hold transactions, and license transfers.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by setting up a clean layout on our whiteboard to tackle ASC 606's five-step revenue recognition model, focusing specifically on complex multi-element arrangements. Given the learner's preference for a concept-first, public lecture style, we will first demystify the core philosophy of revenue recognition: revenue must depict the transfer of promised goods or services to customers in an amount that reflects the consideration to which the entity expects to be entitled. We translate this high-level concept into a visual map of Step 2 (identifying performance obligations) and Step 4 (allocating the transaction price). The teacher should draw two distinct boxes on the left side of the board: one for 'Distinct Goods/Services' and another for 'Combined Output'. This visual anchor helps prevent the common pitfall where candidates fail to separate bundled software and service packages, leading to incorrect front-loaded revenue recognition.

To unpack the mechanics of Step 4, we write out a clear numerical scenario involving a multi-year software arrangement. Imagine a contract where a customer receives a proprietary software license, continuous cloud-based compatibility updates for three years, and premium 24/7 technical support. On the whiteboard, we write down the standalone selling prices (SSP) for each element: License ($100,000), Updates ($30,000), and Support ($20,000), for a total SSP of $150,000. However, the bundle is sold for a transaction price of $120,000. We will walk through the proportional allocation formula, showing how the 20% bundle discount is applied uniformly across all performance obligations unless there is observable evidence that the discount relates to only one or two specific obligations. This breakdown is critical because candidates often struggle with 'hidden' discounts, erroneously applying the entire discount to the software license.

Next, we pivot to the right side of the whiteboard to map out the strict criteria for bill-and-hold transactions. This is a high-frequency testing area where candidates commonly fall into the trap of recognizing revenue when the physical inventory is still sitting in the seller's warehouse without meeting all substantive conditions. We will write out the four-part cumulative test under ASC 606: first, the reason for the bill-and-hold arrangement must be substantive (e.g., the customer requested it because they lack storage space); second, the product must be identified separately as belonging to the customer; third, the product must be ready for physical transfer; and fourth, the seller cannot have the ability to use the product or direct it to another customer. We will illustrate this with a chronological flowchart: the moment control passes versus the moment physical delivery occurs, highlighting how 'control' is the ultimate trigger under the modern standard.

We conclude the session with a hands-on diagnostic practice moment. The teacher will present a scenario where a manufacturer completes a specialized machine but agrees to hold it for three months while the buyer's factory construction is completed. We ask the students to evaluate whether this scenario qualifies for revenue recognition under the bill-and-hold rules. This exercise is designed to reveal whether students can distinguish between a valid business reason (factory under construction) and an invalid one (the seller merely wanting to inflate quarterly sales figures). By tracing the risk and control ownership indicators on our whiteboard diagram, we solidifying their conceptual and analytical foundations before moving on to advanced lease accounting.

tasks: Determine when revenue is recognized in bill-and-hold arrangements.
Allocate transaction price to multi-year software updates and licenses.

sessions.title: Advanced Lease Accounting
sessions.description: Address complex lease transactions, sale-leaseback arrangements, and variable lease payment treatments.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to this whiteboard session on Advanced Lease Accounting. Since the implementation of ASC 842, the boundaries between true asset transfers and lease arrangements have become highly sensitive. Today, we focus on a concept-first, highly illustrative exploration of how the standard prevents companies from using leases as off-balance-sheet financing tricks, specifically looking at sale-leaseback transactions and major lease modifications. Let's start with a blank whiteboard to visually dissect what is actually happening when a company 'sells' an asset and immediately leases it back.

Imagine a company that owns an office building. They need cash, so they sell the building to an investor and sign an agreement to lease it right back. Under ASC 842, we cannot simply take their word that a 'sale' occurred. We must apply the control transfer criteria from ASC 606 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers). On the left side of the board, let's draw two pathways. If control of the asset has not transferred to the buyer-lessor, the transaction is not a sale. Instead, it is a disguised collateralized borrowing. The seller-lessee does not derecognize the asset; they keep it on their books and record a financial liability for the cash received. Students frequently trip up here by trying to record lease assets and liabilities—this is a classic pitfall. We must emphasize that if ASC 606 is not satisfied, it is pure debt, not a lease.

Now, let's look at the right pathway where the transaction does qualify as a sale. On the whiteboard, we will map out the journal entries. The seller-lessee must derecognize the carrying value of the underlying asset, record the cash received, establish the new right-of-use (ROU) asset and lease liability for the leaseback portion, and immediately recognize any gain or loss associated with the completed sale. To bring this to life, we will run through a quick practice exercise where the sale price matches fair value, but then immediately challenge the students: what if the sale price is artificially high? We will draw out how adjustments must be made to treat the excess sale price as additional financing (additional liability) rather than a phantom gain. This prevents companies from inflating their income statement.

Next, let's transition the whiteboard to look at what happens when a lease is already underway and the parties decide to modify it. Lease modifications are notorious on the CPA exam because they require a highly systematic decision tree. Let's draw this tree. The first question is: does the modification grant an additional right of use (such as adding an extra floor of office space) at a price that is commensurate with its standalone selling price? If yes, the modification is treated as an entirely separate, new lease. If no, we must remeasure. We will walk through a scenario where a tenant modifies an existing lease mid-way through its term to extend the duration. We will visually demonstrate how the lessee must recalculate the lease liability using a revised discount rate (the incremental borrowing rate at the date of modification) and make a corresponding adjustment to the ROU asset. This illustrates how modifications act as a structural reset of the accounting estimates.

tasks: Evaluate whether a sale-leaseback transaction qualifies as a sale under ASC 842.
Account for lease modifications that alter the lease term.

sessions.title: Derivatives and Hedge Accounting
sessions.description: Distinguish options, swaps, and futures, and differentiate fair value hedges from cash flow hedges.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing a concept-first foundation for financial derivatives. To demystify these complex instruments, we will draw a clear vertical line on the board to categorize the 'big three' derivatives: options, swaps, and futures. For the general public or a newcomer, we explain a derivative not as a confusing formula, but as a contract whose value is 'derived' from an underlying asset, like a stock or commodity. We will visually map out an option as a paid right (not an obligation) to buy or sell, a swap as a recurring stream of exchange (e.g., swapping a variable interest rate for a fixed one to achieve predictability), and futures as a locked-in, binding obligation to transact in the future. The core concept to emphasize here is how risk is transferred or mitigated through these contracts.

Next, we transition to the main focus: differentiating Fair Value (FV) Hedges from Cash Flow (CF) Hedges. On the left side of the whiteboard, we map out a Fair Value Hedge, explaining that its primary purpose is to protect against changes in the value of an existing asset, liability, or unrecognized firm commitment (such as fixed-rate debt or inventory). On the right side, we map out a Cash Flow Hedge, which protects against the variability of forecasted future cash flows (such as anticipated future purchases or variable-rate interest payments). To make this distinction concrete, we will illustrate a firm commitment to buy equipment in foreign currency next year as a classic exposure to cash flow fluctuation, while holding existing inventory whose price is dropping represents a fair value exposure. This logical split sets up how their accounting entries behave differently in terms of matching.

Now, we dive into the mechanical journal entries for a Fair Value Hedge to show how both the derivative instrument and the hedged item are updated on the balance sheet. On the board, we will write out a side-by-side transaction: on one side, we revalue the physical asset (hedged item) downward due to market decline, debiting Loss and crediting Asset. On the other side, we record the offsetting gain on our derivative contract, debiting the Derivative Asset and crediting Gain. The critical point for students to visualize is that both the gain and loss flow directly into the current period earnings on the Income Statement, perfectly offsetting each other. We will warn students against the common pitfall of forgetting to write down or up the hedged item itself; many candidates mistakenly only record the derivative side, failing to see that the dual-adjustment is what achieves the net zero income effect.

We then shift our visual workspace to contrast the balance sheet treatment of Cash Flow Hedges against Speculative Derivatives. For speculative derivatives (where there is no underlying hedged item and the entity is simply betting on market directions), we write out a direct line showing that all changes in fair value are recognized immediately in current earnings on the Income Statement. For Cash Flow Hedges, however, we draw a path showing that the effective portion of the derivative's gain or loss is initially parked on the Balance Sheet under Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI), completely bypassing the current Income Statement. This temporary resting place prevents earnings volatility until the forecasted transaction actually impacts earnings in the future. We will emphasize the logical chain: we delay matching the hedge results until the actual transaction occurs.

To wrap up the session, we will run through a diagnostic check with the class. We present a scenario where a company enters a derivative to offset the interest volatility of a floating-rate bank loan, but the hedge experiences a small amount of ineffectiveness. We will ask students to identify where the effective and ineffective portions of this cash flow hedge are recognized. This exercise is designed to reveal whether students grasp the difference between the 'matching' principle of hedge accounting and the raw valuation rules. We will explicitly point out that while the effective portion goes to AOCI, any ineffective portion must go straight to current earnings. This reinforces the discipline-level intuition that only a tight, mathematically sound hedge gets the privilege of deferred accounting treatment.

tasks: Prepare journal entries to record a fair value hedge transaction.
Contrast the balance sheet treatment of cash flow hedges vs. speculative derivatives.

sessions.title: Business Combinations
sessions.description: Review pushdown accounting, step acquisitions, contingent consideration, and subsidiary acquisitions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing the foundational timeline of a business combination under ASC 805. The core teaching objective here is to help candidates transition from simple single-step acquisitions to complex transaction structures that involve multi-stage purchases and future performance payouts. On the board, draw a clear horizontal timeline representing the life of an investment, marking the transition point from 'Significant Influence' (using the equity method) to 'Controlling Interest' (requiring full consolidation). This visual anchor is critical because candidates often struggle to realize that gaining control is a significant economic event that triggers a complete revaluation of everything previously held.

Next, we dive into the mechanics of Step Acquisitions. We present a scenario where an investor initially holds a 30% non-controlling interest and later acquires an additional 40% to achieve a 70% controlling stake. The pivotal concept to emphasize is that the acquisition date is the exact day control is achieved, and on this day, the previously held 30% interest must be remeasured to its current fair value. On the whiteboard, map out the journal entry to record this step: debiting the Investment in Subsidiary account to step up its value, and crediting a Gain on Remeasurement in the current period's earnings. A high-frequency pitfall for candidates is forgetting to recognize this gain or loss in earnings, mistakenly trying to adjust equity or carrying forward the old historical cost basis.

From there, we pivot to Contingent Consideration, representing future payouts tied to performance milestones. Draw a decision tree on the board showing the two paths for contingent consideration: Classification as a Liability versus Classification as Equity. Walk through why this distinction dictates all subsequent accounting. When classified as a liability, the contingent payment must be re-measured to fair value at each subsequent reporting date with changes in fair value recognized directly in earnings. When classified as equity, it is not remeasured, and its subsequent settlement is accounted for within equity. Work through an active learning calculation where candidates determine the initial acquisition-date fair value of a revenue-based earn-out using probability-weighted cash flows, showing how this initial estimate directly increases the total consideration transferred and, consequently, impacts the calculation of goodwill.

We then introduce Pushdown Accounting, a concept that often confuses students due to its perspective-shifting nature. On the whiteboard, draw two parallel columns: one representing the Parent's Consolidated Financial Statements and the other representing the Subsidiary's Separate Financial Statements. Explain that pushdown accounting is an option where the subsidiary elects to 'push down' the parent's new acquisition-date fair value basis and goodwill directly onto its own separate balance sheet. Show how this results in a brand-new equity section for the subsidiary, replacing historical retained earnings with a pushdown capital account. This visual side-by-side comparison helps students understand that pushdown accounting does not change consolidated results, but radically alters the subsidiary's standalone ratios and reporting.

To consolidate these concepts, lead the candidates through a comprehensive whiteboard practice problem that synthesizes all these moving parts. The problem scenario involves an entity acquiring a controlling interest in a target company, featuring an existing equity stake that needs remeasurement and a complex contingent earnings liability. Have students calculate the total consideration transferred, remeasure the old equity interest, and compute the resulting goodwill. Explicitly call out how to avoid double-counting or omitting the contingent liability during the goodwill calculation, and highlight how subsequent adjustments to that liability are treated differently depending on whether they occur within the measurement period or afterward as a result of new information.

tasks: Calculate the value of contingent consideration to be recognized at acquisition date.
Record adjustments for a step acquisition that achieves a controlling interest.

sessions.title: Public Company Reporting
sessions.description: Analyze earnings per share (EPS), segment reporting rules, and SEC reporting filings.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core structure of public company reporting, focusing specifically on Earnings Per Share (EPS) and Segment Reporting. Our approach adopts a 'concept-first public lecture' style, designed to unpack the mechanical formulas and thresholds into intuitive, logical frameworks. On the whiteboard, we start by establishing the conceptual divide between Basic EPS and Diluted EPS. Rather than presenting the formulas as cold algebraic fractions, we construct a visualization of a company's capital structure as a scale. On one side, we have actual historical ownership (Basic EPS), and on the other, the potential dilution from 'what-if' scenarios (Diluted EPS). This visual scaffolding prepares the students to understand why potentially dilutive securities (options, warrants, convertible debt) must be evaluated systematically to ensure we only report dilution and never accidental anti-dilution.

Next, we transition into the mechanics of the Treasury Stock Method for options and warrants. Using the whiteboard, the instructor will draw a flow diagram representing the circular logic of this method: first, the 'assumed exercise' of options brings cash into the company; second, the company immediately uses all of that cash to buy back its own shares from the open market at the average market price. The net increase in shares (options exercised minus shares repurchased) becomes the denominator adjustment. We highlight a high-frequency pitfall here: students often forget that if the exercise price is higher than the average market price, the options are out-of-the-money and would actually be anti-dilutive, meaning they are completely excluded from the calculation. By writing out a mock scenario with $50 market price and $40 exercise price versus a $60 exercise price, the visual contrast immediately cements this rule.

To bridge to the second major topic, we pose a question: how do analysts understand what is happening inside a massive, diversified conglomerate? This leads us to Segment Reporting under ASC 280. On the whiteboard, we map out the quantitative threshold rules as a 'three-gate filter'. We draw three large parallel funnels representing the 10% thresholds: the Revenue test (including intersegment sales), the Profit or Loss test (the absolute value of segment profit compared to the greater of combined profitable segments or combined loss segments), and the Assets test. We emphasize that passing any single one of these three tests makes a segment reportable. We walk through a diagnostic matrix of five segments to show how a segment with zero external revenue can still qualify as reportable solely due to significant intersegment transactions or asset holdings.

Finally, we close the loop with the 75% external revenue sufficiency test. We draw a pie chart on the board representing the company's total consolidated external revenue. We show that even after identifying reportable segments using the 10% rules, the combined external revenue of those identified segments must cover at least 75% of the total. If it does not, additional operating segments must be identified and reported, even if they failed the initial 10% tests. This rule-based visual flow transforms what is usually a memorization challenge into a logical, step-by-step diagnostic process that prepares students to tackle both complex multiple-choice questions and task-based simulation structures.

tasks: Calculate diluted earnings per share (EPS) utilizing the treasury stock method.
Identify reportable operating segments based on 10% threshold rules.

sessions.title: State and Local Government Reporting
sessions.description: Analyze the Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) format, reconciliation templates, and government-wide structures.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by visually mapping out the dual-track accounting model that makes state and local government reporting unique. Using the whiteboard, draw two parallel pathways: the bottom pathway representing Governmental Funds (using modified accrual accounting and focusing on current financial resources) and the top pathway representing Government-wide Financial Statements (using full accrual accounting and focusing on economic resources). Emphasize that the core challenge of municipal financial reporting is reconciling these two divergent worlds. Walk through the structural composition of the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR), explaining how the fund-level statements provide granular, short-term budgetary compliance, while the government-wide statements offer a consolidated, long-term operational view. Point out that the reconciliation process is not just a regulatory checkbox but a logical bridge that translates modified cash-like flows into long-term assets and liabilities.

Next, physically draw the reconciliation bridge on the board to establish the conceptual framework for adjusting governmental fund balances to government-wide net position. Use the classic mnemonic 'CANS' (Capital assets, Accumulated depreciation, Non-current liabilities, Service/Internal service fund net position) to guide the adjustments. On the left side of the board, write the starting point: Total Governmental Fund Balance. Beneath it, map out the mechanical additions and subtractions. Explain that because capital assets are expensed under modified accrual rather than capitalized, we must add back the book value of capital assets. Conversely, we must subtract long-term debt because bond issuances are treated as other financing sources instead of liabilities. Address a common candidate pitfall here: many students mistakenly add back bond proceeds because they see them as cash inflows, but in the accrual world, this cash is offset by a long-term liability, resulting in a net-zero impact on net position. Illustrate this transaction flow visually to cement the concept.

Transition the whiteboard focus to the Statement of Revenues, Expenditures, and Changes in Fund Balances and how it reconciles to the government-wide Statement of Activities. Use the mnemonic 'CPAS' (Capital outlays, Principal payments on debt, Asset disposals, Sources of financing/Service funds) to illustrate the logical shifts. Explain that capital expenditures are capitalized on the accrual side, which requires adding back the outlay and subtracting current depreciation expense. Similarly, debt principal retirement, which is an expenditure in fund accounting, must be removed to reflect a reduction in liabilities. Run through a brief active learning scenario where the class must convert a $5,000,000 police station construction expenditure and a $200,000 bond principal payment. This exercise helps students realize how these transactions shift from immediate budget hits to long-term balance sheet items, revealing whether they truly grasp the underlying economic reality.

Finally, dedicate the last major section of the board to Proprietary Funds and their distinct Cash Flow statement format, which differs significantly from the commercial ASC 230 format. Draw a grid comparison showing the four-category governmental cash flow structure: Operating, Noncapital Financing, Capital and Related Financing, and Investing. Emphasize the distinct placement of interest expense and interest income under GASB rules. In commercial accounting, all interest is operating; in government accounting, interest paid on capital debt belongs to Capital and Related Financing, while interest received is classified under Investing. Draw an explicit flow diagram showing where a utility fund’s cash transactions route, prompting students to classify transactions such as customer receipts versus municipal bond interest payments to prevent the frequent pitfall of defaulting to corporate GAAP logic.

tasks: Draft reconciliation lines linking governmental funds to government-wide reporting.
Classify proprietary funds on the Statement of Cash Flows.

projects.stage_title: Conducting Advanced Business Valuation and Performance Analysis
projects.stage_description: Use advanced financial ratios, variance analysis, and forecasting tools to value a target acquisition and evaluate its working capital management strategy.
projects.deliverable_increment: A valuation model sheet added to the main workbook, complete with variance analysis reports and a discounted cash flow (DCF) model.

sections: Covers horizontal/vertical financial analysis, budget flexibility, process costing equivalent units, variable variance calculations, cash conversions, derivatives, business acquisitions, and public company reports.

Determine the valuation of assets under discounted cash flow targets.

units.title: Information Systems and Controls — ISC Discipline
units.description: Explore information security systems, business operations data flows, change management procedures, logical access security, and SOC audit engagements.

lectures.title: Information Systems and Data
lectures.description: Examine operational system components, corporate database configurations, business reporting routines, and system changes.

sessions.title: Information System Components
sessions.description: Understand core hardware, operating software, database architectures, network configurations, and transactional components.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to Unit 5, Session 1. Today we are laying the foundational plumbing of corporate information systems, specifically designed for those approaching this with a concept-first mindset. Under the CPA Evolution model's ISC discipline, understanding the physical and logical layers of IT infrastructure is not just technical trivia; it is the starting point for identifying where financial data can be compromised or altered. We will visually map out these components using our whiteboard, starting with the outer boundaries of a corporate network and drilling down into the core database engines where transactions are finalized.

Let's begin our whiteboard layout by drawing the Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) architecture. To make this intuitive, think of an ERP as a nervous system. I will draw three distinct layers on the board: the Presentation Layer (the user interface on an employee's computer), the Application Layer (the business logic and application servers where rules like credit limit checks are enforced), and the Database Layer (the permanent storage). Students often mistake the user-facing application for the database itself. I will draw a giant red X between the Presentation Layer and the Database Layer to emphasize that users never access the database directly; everything must flow through the Application Layer's security controls. If a user could bypass the application server, they could write unauthorized transactions directly into the ledger.

Now, let's expand our whiteboard schematic to look at the local area network (LAN) configurations that carry this traffic. I will draw a typical office layout with end-user workstations, a local switch, a router, and a firewall connecting them to the cloud-based ERP. Here, we must highlight critical security vulnerabilities. I will draw lightning bolts representing risk vectors at three points: the wireless access point, the connection between the local switch and the router, and the boundary firewall. This visual aids in understanding how unencrypted traffic or weak MAC address filtering allows unauthorized devices to sniff sensitive financial packets before they even reach the database server.

Let's pivot to an active practice moment to test this visual intuition. I want you to look at this network layout and spot the vulnerability: a developer has bypassed the corporate firewall using a personal virtual private network (VPN) client to quickly access an external testing server. Through this exercise, we reveal how a single rogue configuration invalidates all perimeter firewall defenses. We are exposing the 'trusted insider' trap, showing that security is only as strong as its weakest link.

We wrap up by formalizing the definitions of core hardware (servers, storage area networks) and operating systems. The takeaway here is to connect these physical assets to audit risk. If a system's operating software is outdated and unpatched, the integrity of any financial report generated by the ERP above it is compromised. This structured conceptual flow prepares us to transition next into how specific transaction cycles, like revenue and purchasing, actually utilize this very infrastructure.

tasks: Map components of enterprise resource planning (ERP) system layouts.
Identify vulnerabilities within typical local area network configurations.

sessions.title: Business Processes and Information Flows
sessions.description: Trace information flows within revenue, purchase, payroll, and inventory transaction cycles.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by transitioning from theoretical system components to the active pathways where business operations and information systems intersect. On the center of the whiteboard, draw a large circle labeled 'The Transaction Engine' to represent how daily activities generate data. Explain to the audience that in a concept-first framework, business processes are simply structured paths that convert real-world economic events into reliable digital records. We will focus our visual mapping on the expenditure cycle, specifically tracing how a purchase requisition transforms into a final cash disbursement, as this cycle represents one of the most highly tested areas on the CPA Exam for internal control design and audit risk assessment.

Next, begin sketching the system flowchart for the purchase order authorization path. On the left side of the board, draw the 'Originating Department' block, then draw an arrow to the 'Purchasing Department' block, showing the generation of the Purchase Requisition and the subsequent creation of the Purchase Order (PO). Use a different colored marker to draw a branch representing the distribution of this PO: one copy goes to the Vendor, one to Accounts Payable (AP), and a blind copy to the Receiving Dock. Here, explain the critical concept of the 'blind PO'—where quantities are omitted—forcing receiving personnel to physically count incoming inventory rather than simply checking a box. This visual workflow helps students intuitively grasp why system authorizations must be segregated from physical custody and recordkeeping.

Now, expand the flowchart to focus on the Accounts Payable data cycle and introduce the classic 'Three-Way Match' control. Draw three incoming lanes converging at a decision diamond labeled 'Match?'. The three inputs are the Purchase Order (from Purchasing), the Receiving Report (from Receiving), and the Vendor Invoice (from the external vendor). Explain that a failure in any of these matches represents a system exception that must halt the automated payment routine. This is where we address a major student pitfall: candidates frequently confuse the authorization of a purchase with the authorization of a payment. Emphasize that approving a transaction to start is separate from approving the release of corporate cash.

Introduce an interactive diagnostic scenario on the whiteboard by deliberately removing the Receiving Report from the three-way match path. Ask the students to analyze what would happen if a system permitted payment generation based solely on a matching PO and Vendor Invoice. Walk through the logical consequences of this control gap, such as paying for damaged goods that were rejected at the dock, or falling victim to phantom vendor schemes where invoices are submitted for services never rendered. This exercise demonstrates how missing system validations directly translate into material financial statement misstatements, reinforcing both system design and audit risk concepts simultaneously.

Conclude the whiteboard session by summarizing how these transactional flows feed back into the general ledger. Draw a final connection from the matched accounts payable ledger to the overarching financial reporting database. Reiterate that a secure information system must enforce segregation of duties at every handoff point in the flowchart—meaning the individual who authorizes the vendor must never be the individual who signs the digital check or reconciles the bank ledger. This holistic visual mapping ensures students can dissect any transactional system flowchart they encounter on the exam.

tasks: Draft a system flowchart representing the purchase order authorization path.
Identify missing internal control steps within an accounts payable data cycle.

sessions.title: Data Management
sessions.description: Review database structures, relational integrity keys, ETL processes, and analytical queries.
sessions.sessionOutline:
