We begin our exploration of corporate data management by building an intuitive conceptual model of relational databases. Since our learners appreciate a concept-first public lecture style, we will bypass unnecessary database jargon and focus on how a database functions as a structured representation of business reality. Imagine a database as a collection of separate, cleanly organized spreadsheets, or tables, that must reliably talk to one another without repeating data. This is where we introduce the concept of 'normalization'—organizing data to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity. The core foundation of this structure is the 'Primary Key,' a unique identifier (like an Employee ID or a Transaction Number) that ensures no two rows in a table are identical. To connect these tables, we use 'Foreign Keys,' which are primary keys from one table inserted into another to establish a logical relationship, such as linking a Sales Order to a specific Customer ID. 

To make this concrete, the instructor will draw a classic entity-relationship layout on the whiteboard showing an Inventory Table and a Sales Order Detail Table. A common pitfall for candidates is confusing which table gets the foreign key. We will explicitly address this by illustrating the direction of the relationship: the 'one' side of a relationship (such as a unique Inventory Item ID) projects its key as a foreign key into the 'many' side (the Sales Order lines where that item can be purchased multiple times). By visually mapping these connections, learners will grasp how relational integrity prevents orphaned records, ensuring that no sales record can point to an item ID that does not exist in the master inventory.

Next, we transition from static data storage to data movement, introducing the ETL process: Extract, Transform, and Load. In a concept-first framework, we explain ETL as the pipeline that translates raw operational data into clean, analytical insights. 'Extract' pulls raw transactional data from various operational systems. 'Transform' is where the crucial business logic happens—cleansing data, removing duplicates, converting currency types, and structuring it for reporting. Finally, 'Load' imports this polished data into a central data warehouse. We will emphasize why this separation of transactional databases (OLTP) and analytical data warehouses (OLAP) is vital: running heavy queries on a live sales database can slow down daily operations, whereas a dedicated data warehouse is optimized for complex business reporting.

To round out our session with a hands-on application, we will examine a basic SQL (Structured Query Language) query specifically designed to extract inventory valuation records. The instructor will write the syntax on the whiteboard, breaking down the operational anatomy of SELECT, FROM, JOIN, and WHERE clauses. We will show how a SELECT statement specifies the inventory item name, how a JOIN clause brings together the inventory quantities table and unit cost table using their primary/foreign key relationship, and how a WHERE clause filters for active stock. Our practice walkthrough will challenge students to trace this SQL query and identify the exact logic used to calculate total extended valuation (Quantity multiplied by Cost). This exercises their analytical skills, preparing them to interpret query logic and system-generated reports on the CPA exam without getting bogged down in coding minutiae.

tasks: Identify primary keys and foreign keys in database tables.
Examine an SQL query used to extract inventory valuation records.

sessions.title: System Development and Change Management
sessions.description: Study SDLC phases, testing protocols (user acceptance testing), segregation of duties, and release controls.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by sketching a horizontal pipeline across the whiteboard to represent the life of software from its initial inception to its active use. This visualization is essential for establishing the foundation of the Systems Development Life Cycle (SDLC) and Change Management. By walking students through the sequence of Planning, Analysis, Design, Development, Testing, Implementation, and Maintenance, we ground the technical concepts in a logical flow. The primary objective is to help candidates realize that system development is not a chaotic process of writing code on the fly, but a highly regulated journey designed to mitigate operational risk. We want to emphasize that each phase serves as a structural gatekeeper, ensuring that only thoroughly vetted updates make it to the core system.

Next, we pivot to a deep-dive exploration of segregated environments, which is a frequent source of confusion on the CPA exam. On the whiteboard, we draw three distinct, isolated boxes labeled 'Development', 'Test/QA (Quality Assurance)', and 'Production'. We explain the logical firewall between these zones, illustrating why developers write and run code only in the Development environment, why independent testers use the Test/QA sandbox, and why the live business transactions occur exclusively in Production. The critical concept here is that developers should never have write access to the Production environment, and real business users should not operate in the Development zone. This isolation is crucial for protecting data integrity and preventing untested code from disrupting live operations.

To make this concrete, we introduce the formal workflow for promoting code. We draw arrows from Development to Test, and then to Production, highlighting the mandatory controls at each boundary. We explain that before any code can move, a formal Change Request must be authorized. We then walk through User Acceptance Testing (UAT), where actual business users verify that the system functions as expected. We illustrate that code promotion must be executed by an independent Release Manager or System Administrator, rather than the developer who wrote it. We explicitly warn candidates about the common exam trap of assuming that a developer's self-testing is sufficient for deployment, emphasizing that independent validation and formal approval are non-negotiable.

Finally, we address the strict Segregation of Duties (SoD) in IT environments by drawing a line down the center of the whiteboard, separating 'Developers' from 'Operations/System Operators'. We explain the inherent conflict of interest when an individual has both the power to write code and the authority to deploy it to live systems, which creates a massive risk of unauthorized or fraudulent changes. We challenge the students with a diagnostic scenario where a small company allows its chief developer to bypass the promotion process during an emergency outage. Through this exercise, we guide students to identify the control failure and explain how a separate operator must perform the deployment, even under emergency procedures, to maintain proper internal control and accountability.

tasks: Identify the correct steps to move code from development to production.
Explain how segregation of duties is maintained between developers and system operators.

sessions.title: IT Operations
sessions.description: Understand batch vs. real-time processing, job scheduling, and operational performance metrics.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back to Unit 5. Today, we are exploring the heartbeat of enterprise systems: IT Operations. Under the CPA Evolution model, candidates must grasp how transactional data is captured, scheduled, and maintained. Our focus centers on the core operational choice: Batch vs. Real-Time Processing (OLTP), alongside the system architectures that govern job scheduling and error resolution. Because the student prefers a concept-first, public lecture style, we will skip overly technical jargon and instead anchor these architectures in vivid, real-world operational scenarios. Let's start on the whiteboard by drawing two parallel conveyor belts representing data processing paths.

First, we sketch the Batch Processing pipeline. We draw individual transactions landing in a 'Holding Bin' throughout the day, which are accumulated and processed together at a scheduled off-peak time, such as midnight. Explain to students that batch processing is highly efficient for large volumes of similar transactions where immediate feedback is not required—such as corporate payroll, end-of-month reconciliations, or daily credit card interest calculations. The primary benefit is lower processing costs and reduced strain on main systems during business hours. However, the critical drawback is the 'information lag.' A common pitfall for candidates on the exam is assuming that batch systems are simply outdated. We must clarify that they are highly strategic; they are chosen intentionally to preserve computational resources when real-time updates serve no immediate operational purpose.

Next, on the other side of the board, we contrast this with Real-Time Processing, or Online Transaction Processing (OLTP). Draw immediate, bidirectional arrows going from a user terminal directly into a 'Live Database' with no holding bin in between. This is the model used for airline reservation systems, live inventory checkouts, and ATM withdrawals where instant validation and immediate data consistency are non-negotiable. Point out that the tradeoff here is high resource consumption and the constant threat of database locking or performance degradation during peak hours. Emphasize that in a real-time environment, system downtime or network disruptions result in immediate business interruption, whereas batch runs can often be delayed or rescheduled with minimal customer-facing impact.

Now, let's look at the nervous system of these processing runs: Job Scheduling and the error resolution paths. On the whiteboard, map out a scheduled interface sequence—such as a daily retail sales file being transferred from point-of-sale systems to the main corporate ledger. Draw a decision tree showing what happens when a scheduled job succeeds versus when it fails due to network disconnects or dirty data. Walk through the concept of 'automated recovery' versus 'manual intervention' paths. This introduces a great practice exercise: challenge the students to trace a scenario where a mid-run batch job fails due to an out-of-balance account entry. Have them identify the risk of partial execution—where some ledger accounts are updated while others are not—and discuss why automatic rollback features and detailed error logs are essential controls that auditors look for to ensure completeness and accuracy.

tasks: Compare real-time online transaction processing (OLTP) with end-of-day batch runs.
Examine error resolution paths in scheduled interface processes.

lectures.title: IT Governance and Security
lectures.description: Covers framework configurations, security policies, identity controls, cybersecurity protections, and disaster backup plans.

sessions.title: IT Governance
sessions.description: Learn framework structures such as COBIT, corporate alignment strategies, risk assessments, and executive policies.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome students to Unit 5, Lecture 2, Session 1. Today, we are laying the groundwork for Information Systems and Controls (ISC) by dissecting IT Governance. For learners approaching this from a concept-first, public-lecture style, our primary objective is to demystify how massive corporate structures prevent their IT systems from operating in a silo. We begin by drawing a visual hierarchy on the whiteboard. At the very top, we place 'Corporate Strategy and Risk Appetite,' and at the bottom, we place 'Daily IT Operations.' The core mission of IT Governance is to build the bridging mechanisms—specifically frameworks and policies—that ensure technology investments directly support business goals while mitigating systemic risks.

To make this concrete, we introduce the COBIT framework (Control Objectives for Information and Related Technology). On the whiteboard, we map out its core philosophy: separating 'Governance' (which evaluates, directs, and monitors) from 'Management' (which plans, builds, runs, and monitors). A common pitfall for candidates is treating these two terms as interchangeable synonyms. We prevent this misunderstanding by illustrating a clear feedback loop on the board. We show that governance is the domain of the Board of Directors, establishing the overall 'rules of the road' and risk tolerances, while management is the domain of executive leadership (like the CIO) executing tactics within those boundaries.

Next, we pivot to aligning IT strategies with a company's specific risk tolerance profile. Imagine a conservative regional bank versus a rapid-growth fintech startup. On the whiteboard, we construct a contrast matrix. For the conservative bank, the risk appetite is low, meaning governance policies must prioritize strict access controls and zero-trust baselines over deployment speed. For the startup, the risk appetite might allow for faster deployment cycles, but still requires guardrails to avoid regulatory non-compliance. We walk students through how an organization translates these risk profiles into enforceable IT Acceptable-Use Policies (AUP). We explain that an AUP isn't just human resources boilerplate; it is a foundational administrative control that legally and operationally defines what actions are permitted on corporate assets.

We conclude this session with an interactive scenario-based exercise to test conceptual alignment. We present a case where a company's business goal is to transition to remote-first work, but their existing IT security strategy prohibits off-site database access. Students are asked to resolve this friction. This exercise is designed to reveal whether learners can identify the disconnect between strategic business goals and rigid, unaligned IT rules. We guide them to see that effective governance doesn't simply say 'no' to mitigate risk; instead, it adapts security structures—such as implementing secure VPNs and virtual desktop infrastructures—to safely enable the business strategy.

tasks: Align IT security strategies with a corporate risk tolerance profile.
Evaluate components of an IT acceptable-use policy.

sessions.title: IT Risks and General Controls
sessions.description: Examine IT general controls (ITGCs) and application-level verification controls.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session on the whiteboard by drawing a large, conceptual map of an enterprise technology stack. Use the visual metaphor of a secure fortress to establish the fundamental division between IT General Controls (ITGCs) and Application Controls. Explain that ITGCs represent the foundation and outer defenses of the fortress—such as change management, network security, and computer operations—which apply across all systems. Conversely, Application Controls are the specialized locks and automated checks inside specific rooms, like accounting or payroll modules. By presenting this visual contrast early, we demystify the technical jargon for students coming from non-technical backgrounds, helping them intuitively understand why an application control is only as reliable as the underlying ITGC environment supporting it.

Transition to mapping out the core domains of ITGCs on the whiteboard, focusing on the lifecycle of system changes and operations. Explain the pipeline of Change Management: moving code from a separate development environment, to testing/quality assurance, and finally to production. Highlight the critical risk of 'developer bypass' where an engineer has access to both write code and push it to production. Discuss how a breakdown in these foundational controls invalidates the integrity of all automated business processes underneath. Address a common student pitfall here: candidates often mistake an application error, such as a miscalculated depreciation run, as an isolated software bug, when the root cause is actually an ITGC failure in the system development or change management process that allowed untested code to run.

Next, drill down into Application-level Verification Controls, focusing on transaction processing inputs. On the whiteboard, draw a mock user-interface for an invoice processing screen. Walk through the concept of 'garbage-in, garbage-out' and explain how input validation controls serve as the primary automated gatekeeper. Define and illustrate key input validation techniques such as limit checks, range checks, format checks, and completeness checks. To anchor this concept, demonstrate how an input field without a limit check could allow an accidental extra zero to turn a $10,000 inventory purchase into a $100,000 balance sheet error, showing that these controls are not just technical nuances but critical components of financial reporting accuracy.

Conclude with a collaborative whiteboard workshop designed to apply these concepts to real-world scenarios. Present a case study of a mid-sized retail company where developers occasionally help with database maintenance in production and warehouse managers manually override bulk inventory receipts without system logs. Challenge the students to identify these specific ITGC vulnerabilities and trace their downstream impacts on financial audits. Finally, guide the students through a step-by-step design exercise where they draft a multi-tiered input validation framework for the company's transaction pipeline, incorporating format, limit, and master-file verification checks to ensure total data integrity before processing.

tasks: Identify ITGC vulnerabilities in a case study scenario.
Design an input validation check for transaction processing.

sessions.title: Logical Access Controls
sessions.description: Analyze multi-factor authentication (MFA), role-based access controls (RBAC), and user provisioning procedures.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing the core distinction between physical and logical access controls. Using the analogy of a bank vault, physical access prevents unauthorized people from entering the building, whereas logical access controls prevent them from accessing the software systems and data stored inside, even if they are physically present. The instructor should write the 'Principle of Least Privilege' at the top of the whiteboard, highlighting that logical access is not about enabling access, but limiting it to only what is absolutely necessary for an individual's job function. This concept-first setup reframes access control from a tech hurdle into an essential protective shield for internal system integrity.

Next, the instructor will visually map out Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) on the whiteboard. Instead of diving straight into tech jargon, explain MFA through three categories: something you know (like a password), something you have (like a physical token or phone), and something you are (like a fingerprint). The instructor will draw a simple diagram showing a user attempting to cross three distinct safety checkpoints, explaining that using two factors of the same category (e.g., a password and a PIN) does not constitute MFA. A key pitfall to address here is 'MFA fatigue' or social engineering, where attackers bombard users with notifications until they click approve. This demonstrates that MFA is not an absolute cure-all, but a layer of security that relies on proper user awareness.

Transitioning from authentication (proving who you are) to authorization (proving what you can do), we introduce Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). The instructor will sketch an organizational chart on the board and contrast RBAC with individual user permissions. Explain that mapping permissions directly to individuals creates administrative chaos and security gaps. Instead, we map permissions to roles (like 'Accounts Payable Clerk'), and then assign users to those roles. This is where we introduce the first practice scenario: drafting a Segregation of Duties (SoD) matrix. The instructor will draw a grid on the whiteboard with roles on one axis and critical system privileges (e.g., Create Vendor, Approve Invoice, Authorize Payment) on the other. Walk through why a single role must never have access to overlapping parts of this transaction cycle, emphasizing how this matrix serves as an audit-ready visual tool to prevent fraud.

We then shift focus to the identity lifecycle, commonly called the 'Joiner-Mover-Leaver' framework. The instructor will draw a timeline on the board representing an employee's career path. Special emphasis should be placed on 'Movers'—employees who change departments. Explain the high-frequency pitfall of 'privilege creep,' where a promoted employee retains all their old administrative privileges alongside their new ones. This sets up our final practice task: establishing a robust, immediate offboarding protocol for 'Leavers' with elevated credentials, such as system administrators. The instructor will walk through a step-by-step workflow on the board, demonstrating why terminating access in active directory must occur simultaneously with physical termination to prevent hostile insider retaliation.

tasks: Draft a matrix aligning system roles with segregation of duties parameters.
Determine appropriate procedures for offboarding employees with elevated credentials.

sessions.title: Cybersecurity
sessions.description: Understand threats: malware, phishing, ransomware, zero-day vulnerabilities, network firewalls, and encryption (symmetric vs. asymmetric).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing a basic conceptual hierarchy of cybersecurity threats before moving into technical defenses. The core goal is to shift learners from a passive 'terminology-memorization' mindset to an active 'threat-modeling' perspective, matching their request for a concept-first public lecture style. The lecture opens by illustrating a classic bank vault analogy: physical security relies on walls and guards, whereas digital security relies on access control and cryptographic boundaries. We map out the landscape of threats on the left side of the whiteboard, categorizing them into social engineering vector (phishing), malicious software vectors (malware and ransomware), and systemic technical windows (zero-day vulnerabilities). By contrasting phishing (exploiting the human element to gain initial entry) with ransomware (the actual payload that encrypts files for extortion), students see how attackers chain different exploits together. This prevents the common pitfall of treating these threats as isolated, mutually exclusive multiple-choice terms.

Once the threat landscape is established, we pivot to the first major defensive mechanism on the center board: network firewalls and Intrusion Detection/Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS). We draw a network perimeter layout showing an external untrusted network, a demilitarized zone (DMZ), and a trusted internal database network. The instructor illustrates how a firewall acts as a security guard reading a manifest (packet-filtering based on IP and ports) while an IDS acts as a security camera system analyzing behavior. We walk through a practical scenario where a signature-based IDS flags a known malware pattern versus an anomaly-based IDS flagging an unusual volume of database queries at midnight. This concrete contrast helps candidates intuitively grasp how modern monitoring tools identify network threats in real time.

Next, we transition to the cryptographic heart of the lecture, focusing on the fundamental mechanisms of encryption: symmetric versus asymmetric. On the right side of the whiteboard, we construct a parallel visual walkthrough. For symmetric encryption, we draw a single key ('the shared secret') used for both locking and unlocking a box containing data, noting its high speed but extreme key distribution vulnerability. Directly below it, we diagram asymmetric encryption using two separate keys: a widely distributed Public Key to lock the box, and a closely guarded Private Key held only by the recipient to unlock it. The instructor highlights the critical math-based relationship between these keys to debunk the common misconception that a public key can be used to decrypt a message it just encrypted.

We conclude the whiteboard session with an active-learning check. The instructor presents a scenario where a company needs to secure bulk transactional data storage while also establishing a secure communication channel with a new external vendor over the public internet. Learners are asked to determine where symmetric encryption is preferred (for massive, local data stores due to computational efficiency) and where asymmetric encryption is mandatory (for establishing initial handshakes and key exchanges without a secure pre-existing physical channel). This exercise forces students to synthesize both efficiency and security trade-offs, cementing their conceptual framework for the CPA Exam's practical IT scenarios.

tasks: Differentiate symmetric and asymmetric encryption mechanisms.
Explain how intrusion detection systems (IDS) identify network threats.

sessions.title: Incident Response and Recovery
sessions.description: Examine disaster recovery plans (DRPs), backup protocols, and business continuity planning (BCP).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard-focused session by introducing the fundamental tension between business continuity planning (BCP) and disaster recovery planning (DRP). Teachers should visually anchor this on the board by sketching a broad corporate umbrella labeled 'BCP' (focused on keeping business operations functional during a disruption) and drawing a specific technical pillar underneath labeled 'DRP' (focused on restoring IT systems, infrastructure, and data). Many candidates mistakenly treat these terms as interchangeable; our goal is to show that DRP is the technical execution branch of the broader business resilience strategy.

Next, the whiteboard illustration transitions to the core technical metrics that govern all disaster recovery strategies: Recovery Point Objective (RPO) and Recovery Time Objective (RTO). Draw a horizontal timeline representing a disaster event. To the left of the disaster point, draw an arrow pointing backward in time to represent RPO—the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time (e.g., hours of transactions lost). To the right of the disaster point, draw an arrow pointing forward to represent RTO—the maximum acceptable downtime before systems must be restored. It is crucial to address the frequent pitfall where students confuse the direction of these metrics; emphasize that RPO looks backward to data backups, while RTO looks forward to system restoration.

Now, build a comparative matrix on the whiteboard to analyze the three main types of recovery sites: cold, warm, and hot. For the 'Cold Site', sketch an empty warehouse shell with electricity and physical space but absolutely no hardware or data, requiring days or weeks to activate. For the 'Warm Site', add pre-configured hardware and network connections but without real-time data replication, requiring hours or days to restore. For the 'Hot Site', draw a mirrored replica of the production environment with continuous real-time data replication, ready to take over operations almost instantly (seconds or minutes). Guide the students to see that as recovery speed increases, the cost of the solution rises exponentially, requiring a strategic balance based on business criticality.

To apply these concepts practically, present an interactive design scenario. Suppose a financial transaction platform has an RPO of 1 hour and an RTO of 4 hours. Walk the students through evaluating different backup frequency profiles (differential vs. incremental backups) and site types to meet these parameters. Explain that a cold site would fail the 4-hour RTO, and simple weekly backups would catastrophically breach the 1-hour RPO. This exercise highlights how RPO and RTO dictate technical decisions, ensuring students learn to architect solutions rather than just memorize definitions.

tasks: Differentiate cold, warm, and hot recovery sites.
Design backup frequency profiles to meet a defined Recovery Point Objective (RPO).

sessions.title: Privacy and Confidentiality
sessions.description: Review regulatory parameters: GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA, and data classifications.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the final session of our IT Governance and Security lecture, where we transition from securing infrastructure to protecting the sensitive data that resides within it. To set the stage, begin by drawing a clear distinction on the whiteboard between data security and data privacy. Explain that while security focuses on keeping unauthorized users out of the system, privacy dictates how personal data is collected, processed, and protected in compliance with legal mandates. On the left side of the whiteboard, sketch a data classification pyramid. Label the levels from bottom to top: Public, Internal Use, Confidential, and Restricted. Walk through how modern enterprises map their data assets to this pyramid, highlighting that classification dictates the level of control required under the AICPA Trust Services Criteria.

Next, build a comparative regulatory matrix on the center of the whiteboard to unpack GDPR, HIPAA, and CCPA. Address the absolute core concepts of each framework, ensuring candidates understand their distinct jurisdictions and scopes. Under GDPR, emphasize the 'right to be forgotten' and how it applies to any organization globally processing EU citizens' data. For CCPA, focus on consumer rights regarding the sale of personal information in California. For HIPAA, isolate Protected Health Information (PHI) within healthcare environments. A high-frequency pitfall here is when candidates confuse general corporate confidentiality with these strict privacy mandates. Explicitly clarify that general confidentiality protects corporate intellectual property, whereas privacy specifically protects the data of individuals.

Now, transition to the first practical whiteboard visual: a raw database layout containing columns such as Customer_ID, First_Name, IP_Address, Zip_Code, and Purchase_Amount. Invite the class to trace which elements constitute Personally Identifiable Information (PII). This is a critical diagnostic moment. Many students falsely believe only sensitive national identifiers like Social Security Numbers qualify as PII. Use a red marker to circle 'IP_Address' and 'Zip_Code,' explaining that under modern standards, these are considered indirect or quasi-identifiers because they can be combined with other public datasets to uniquely identify an individual. Detail the logical chain of 'linkability' and why identifying linkable data is the first step in any robust compliance audit.

Once the PII has been mapped, pivot the whiteboard demonstration to protection strategies, specifically contrasting Data Masking, Tokenization, and Encryption. Draw an input/output flow diagram to illustrate how dynamic data masking transforms a real credit card number into a masked variant (e.g., asterisks hiding all but the last four digits) before displaying it to a customer service agent. Draw a second flow to contrast this with tokenization, where sensitive data is replaced by a non-sensitive surrogate value (token) while the real data is securely vaulted. Warn candidates of a common audit oversight: applying masking in a user interface while leaving the underlying database queries unmasked, which leaves the system highly vulnerable to unauthorized internal exposure.

Conclude the session with a tactical scenario exercise. Ask the class to evaluate a situation where a software developer requests production data to troubleshoot an active bug. Walk through the correct auditing workflow: instead of granting raw database access, the organization must implement pseudonymization or data scrubbing techniques to strip away all PII beforehand. This ensures compliance with both the GDPR minimization principle and SOC 2 privacy criteria. Sum up by linking these privacy architectures directly back to the overall IT governance strategy, ensuring students leave with a holistic understanding of how privacy laws dictate technical engineering decisions.

tasks: Identify personal identifiable information (PII) elements in a database layout.
Assess data masking techniques for compliance audits.

lectures.title: System and Organization Controls
lectures.description: Deep dive into SOC reporting standards, Trust Services Criteria, and procedures for reviewing service organization reports.

sessions.title: SOC Engagement Fundamentals
sessions.description: Define the purpose, structure, and differences of SSAE 18 SOC reporting packages.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing why System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports exist, framing them through a simple outsourcing dilemma that any business leader faces. When an enterprise hands over its payroll processing, cloud hosting, or data management to a third-party service provider, it cannot simply trust that the vendor's internal controls are working. However, sending dozens of external auditors to crawl through the vendor's data center every year is highly inefficient. To solve this friction, we introduce the concept of a single independent auditor examining the vendor once and publishing a standardized report that all client auditors can rely upon under the SSAE 18 framework.

On the left side of the whiteboard, draw a three-part comparative matrix to break down the distinct objectives of SOC 1, SOC 2, and SOC 3. This visual hierarchy is crucial because candidates frequently confuse the targets of these audits. Write 'SOC 1 = Financial Focus (ICFR)' at the top, explaining that this report directly supports the audit of a user entity's financial statements by validating controls over transactional integrity, billing, or ledger balances. Directly beneath it, write 'SOC 2 = Operational Security & Trust (TSC)', explaining that this is geared toward IT security, compliance officers, and operations teams who need to evaluate data integrity and safety without necessarily auditing financial systems. Finally, draw a line to 'SOC 3 = Public Trust', and describe it as a highly redacted, general-use marketing document that omits detailed test descriptions so it can be freely distributed to the public.

Transitioning to the right side of the whiteboard, construct a chronological timeline to address the second core pillar: the structural difference between Type 1 and Type 2 reports. Draw a single point in time—a specific date like 'as of October 31'—to represent Type 1. Explain that a Type 1 report is merely a snapshot evaluating the design and implementation of controls on that exact day. It answers whether the doors have locks, but not whether employees kept them locked over time. Now, draw a horizontal block representing a continuous window—typically a six-month minimum period—to represent Type 2. Explain that Type 2 evaluates not only design and implementation but also the operational effectiveness of those controls over that entire duration.

Address a critical trap that candidates fall into: assuming that a Type 2 report is always better or that a SOC 2 report is superior to a SOC 1 report. Explain that these are not progressive upgrades but different tools for different jobs. A user auditor reviewing financial statements cannot substitute a SOC 2 for a SOC 1, even if the SOC 2 is a Type 2 report, because the underlying control objectives must match the financial assertions of the user entity. Similarly, a Type 1 report is often used as a baseline for new systems or during a transition phase, whereas a Type 2 is mandatory for ongoing assurance.

Conclude with a simulated whiteboard analysis exercise. Sketch a scenario involving a cloud-based inventory manager that experienced an unannounced system update during the year. Ask the students to determine which report would expose the failure of change management controls during that update. Walk them through the logic that a Type 1 report would likely miss this if the update happened outside its single-point assessment date, while a Type 2 report's continuous testing window would capture the operational lapse. This concrete illustration reinforces why the distinction between a point-in-time design review and a historical execution test is so vital for audit planning.

tasks: Compare SOC 1, SOC 2, and SOC 3 engagement objectives.
Differentiate a Type 1 report from a Type 2 report.

sessions.title: SOC 1 Engagements
sessions.description: Focus on evaluating controls relevant to a user entity's internal control over financial reporting (ICFR).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by establishing the critical link between outsourced services and a user entity's financial statements. Since the learner has opted for a concept-first, public-lecture style, we must avoid dry checklists and instead paint a vivid conceptual picture: when a company outsources its payroll or cloud-based general ledger to a third party, the auditors of that company cannot simply blindfold themselves to what happens inside that third-party's black box. This is where SOC 1, governed by SSAE 18, comes in. On the whiteboard, draw a clear boundary line dividing the 'User Entity' (the client being audited) and the 'Service Organization' (the service provider). Explain that a SOC 1 report is explicitly designed to address controls that are relevant to the user entity's Internal Control over Financial Reporting (ICFR). 

Now, let's map how financial assertions travel across this boundary. Write the core financial assertions—such as Accuracy, Completeness, and Valuation—on the board. If the service organization processes transactions, any failure in their system directly threatens these assertions on the user entity's financial statements. For instance, if a payroll provider has a system bug that miscalculates withholding taxes, the user entity's liabilities and expenses will be inaccurate. Point out a common student pitfall here: candidates often confuse SOC 1 with SOC 2, assuming that any system error is an IT or security issue under SOC 2. Emphasize that if an IT control failure directly corrupts financial numbers, it falls squarely under the jurisdiction of a SOC 1 evaluation. 

Next, transition the whiteboard visual to a concrete, high-frequency testing scenario: automated matching functions within a billing or inventory system. Draw a flowchart showing an incoming purchase order, a receiving report, and a vendor invoice. In an automated system, software matches these three documents before generating a payment journal entry. To test this automated control, an auditor cannot merely look at a paper file; they must formulate testing methods that challenge the system's logic. Explain the logic of 'test data' techniques—where the auditor inputs intentional errors (like mismatched quantities or unauthorized prices) into a staging environment to verify if the automated matching system flags and rejects the transaction. This hands-on illustration helps students transition from abstract control theory to concrete, application-level audit procedures.

Conclude the session with an interactive practice prompt that challenges the instructor to poll the classroom or prompt the viewer: 'If we find that the automated matching system failed to flag a $50,000 discrepancy during our test run, which specific financial statement assertion is compromised, and what is our immediate next step as the auditor?' This question forces learners to connect the technical test method back to the foundational assertion of Valuation and Accuracy, reinforcing the closed-loop nature of SOC 1 evaluation before transitioning to non-financial SOC 2 criteria in the next session.

tasks: Identify key financial assertions evaluated in a SOC 1 report.
Formulate testing methods for automated matching functions.

sessions.title: SOC 2 Engagements
sessions.description: Examine the evaluation of non-financial controls using the Trust Services Criteria (TSC) structure.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by visually sketching the core domain of a SOC 2 engagement on the whiteboard, contrasting it directly with the financial reporting boundaries of SOC 1. The teacher must emphasize that SOC 2 focuses on non-financial operational controls under the Trust Services Criteria (TSC). On the left side of the board, draw a clear boundary representing a client's data storage, and on the right side, draw the Cloud Service Provider's (CSP) multi-tenant architecture. The primary goal is to establish that SOC 2 is not about reconciling ledger balances; it is about verifying the operational integrity, safety, and privacy of systems that handle sensitive customer information.

Transition next into a conceptual deep dive into how a cloud host meets security guidelines within a SOC 2 framework. Draw a logical sequence of defenses starting with perimeter firewalls, moving inward to identity and access management (IAM), and finally reaching database encryption. The core logical link here is that security serves as the baseline 'common criteria' that must be met before any other TSC criteria are evaluated. To prevent the common misconception that a SOC 2 report is a simple checklist or a technical 'pass/fail' certificate, the teacher should explain how examiners look for a design and operational philosophy that matches the specific risk profile of the entity. Introduce a mini-scenario where a cloud host's automated patch management protocol has a minor operational gap; explain how the auditor notes this exception without necessarily failing the entire control framework.

Now, draw a second visual zone on the whiteboard to address a major challenge in audit prep: evaluating scope limitations within sample engagement planning documents. Walk through how to identify the boundaries of what is included versus what is excluded from the system description (such as third-party subservice organizations). On the board, write out 'In-Scope: Co-Location Facility A' and 'Out-of-Scope: Disaster Recovery Site B.' Instruct the teacher to guide students through the logic of why an excluded subservice organization could leave a gaping vulnerability in the user entity's security posture. This exercise is designed to reveal if students can critically spot when a service organization has restricted the scope of the audit too tightly to mask weak operational controls.

Wrap up the session with an interactive practice scenario. Present a draft system description of a cloud hosting provider that excludes their database backup servers from the SOC 2 audit scope. Ask the students to evaluate whether this scope limitation is acceptable and how it affects the utility of the resulting SOC 2 report for an enterprise client. The teacher will unpack how this scope exclusion compromises the overall security and availability assertions, illustrating that a SOC 2 report is only as strong as its weakest scoped boundary.

tasks: Assess how a cloud host meets security guidelines in a SOC 2 review.
Analyze scope limitations in sample engagement planning documents.

sessions.title: Trust Services Criteria
sessions.description: Master the details of the five criteria: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome back to our exploration of System and Organization Controls. Today, we are focusing on the visual and logical mapping of the AICPA's five Trust Services Criteria: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy. Because our student prefers a concept-first, public lecture style, we will skip dense jargon-heavy slides and instead construct a comprehensive visual framework on our whiteboard. We will start with a single core system diagram and layer these five criteria over it. Students often struggle to differentiate among these criteria under pressure—especially separating confidentiality from privacy, and processing integrity from availability. Today, we will demystify these distinctions.

Let's begin by drawing a standard service organization architecture on the whiteboard: a client's data enters through an input portal, processes within a central database engine, stores in a system repository, and is transmitted back to the user or stored securely. To introduce the first and only mandatory criterion, 'Security' (often referred to as the common criteria), we draw a protective shield surrounding this entire pipeline. We explain to the class that Security acts as the foundation because it protects the system against unauthorized access and damage. If a malicious actor breaches the firewall, none of the other criteria can be guaranteed. The teacher should highlight that security controls—such as multi-factor authentication, firewalls, and intrusion detection systems—are the prerequisites for the remaining four criteria.

Now, let's layer on 'Availability.' We draw a clock icon next to our data repository. Availability asks a simple question: Is the system operational and usable for the client when they expect it to be? The primary trap students fall into is confusing a system crash with a security failure; while they can be related, a system going offline due to high traffic is purely an availability issue. To demonstrate this, we will map a standard data backup schedule to this criterion. On the whiteboard, we draw incremental and full backup nodes branching off our repository. Backups do not keep hackers out (Security), but they do guarantee that if the primary system fails, operational state can be restored quickly, satisfying the Availability criterion. We will also illustrate disaster recovery sites and redundant servers here to show how resilience ensures continuous uptime.

Next, we write 'Processing Integrity' inside our central database engine on the board. This criterion ensures that system processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized. To illustrate this concept, we sketch a simple transactional processing pipeline: a purchase order enters the system, undergoes automated matching against a receiving report, and updates the inventory ledger. If the system processes only half of the order, or associates it with the wrong customer, processing integrity is breached even if the system remains 100% online (Availability) and completely secure (Security). We will map input validation checks, automated reconcilement routines, and error-correction logs to this box. This demonstrates to the students that processing integrity is about the quality and accuracy of the data processing life cycle.

Finally, we address the common point of confusion: 'Confidentiality' versus 'Privacy.' On the left side of our board under Confidentiality, we write 'Business-to-Business Data' (such as intellectual property, price lists, or pending transaction details). On the right side under Privacy, we write 'Personally Identifiable Information' or PII (such as Social Security Numbers, medical records, or credit card details of individual consumers). Confidentiality is about restricting access to proprietary business information based on agreements, using encryption and non-disclosure controls. Privacy, however, specifically deals with how personal information is collected, used, retained, disclosed, and disposed of, directly aligning with the AICPA's Generally Accepted Privacy Principles (GAPP). We can visually connect this on our board by showing a proprietary algorithm encrypted under Confidentiality, contrasted with an employee's tax file handled under Privacy, which requires consent and deletion rights. This visual distinction prevents students from misidentifying these two highly tested areas on the exam.

tasks: Map a service organization's backup schedule to the availability criterion.
Identify controls that support the processing integrity criterion.

sessions.title: Evaluating SOC Reports
sessions.description: Learn to read SOC opinions, analyze exceptions, and address Complementary User Entity Controls (CUECs).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin today's session by visually mapping the relationship between the service organization and the user entity on our whiteboard. Many students mistakenly assume that a service organization's SOC report acts as a 'clean bill of health' that absolves the user entity of any control responsibilities. To dispel this early, we draw a clear physical boundary on the board: on the left is the Service Organization (such as a cloud-based payroll vendor), and on the right is the User Entity (the client). Connecting them is a bridging bridge labeled 'Complementary User Entity Controls' (CUECs). The core concept here is that a SOC report is only valid if the user entity has built their own internal matching controls to connect with the output of the service organization. If the service organization promises secure processing, but the client does not restrict administrative access to the input portal, the entire internal control environment collapses.

Next, we build a workflow diagram focusing on the anatomy of a payroll processing system to bring CUECs to life. We outline a real-world scenario where a company outsources payroll calculations to a third-party vendor. On the whiteboard, we write down specific CUECs that the user entity must implement: verifying the authorized employee list before submitting data, reviewing transaction registers to catch discrepancies, and managing secure user credentials on their own local network. This visual breakdown demonstrates that controls do not exist in a vacuum. It forces students to realize that even if a service organization receives an unmodified (clean) opinion, the user auditor cannot rely on it if the user entity neglects these complementary responsibilities.

Moving on to the evaluation of the actual opinion in the SOC report, we map out the four possible reporting opinions on our whiteboard: Unmodified, Modified/Qualified, Adverse, and Disclaimer. We deep dive into how an auditor analyzes exceptions found within the body of a Type 2 report. We draw a ledger detailing a hypothetical 'Exception' where 3 out of 45 sampled changes to firewall rules lacked proper authorization. We walk through the logical chain: Is this exception systemic or isolated? Did it result in an actual security breach? We teach students to analyze the management's response to the exception and evaluate if mitigating controls existed to limit the overall risk.

Finally, we address the critical decision-making process for a user auditor when faced with a qualified SOC report opinion. We draw a decision tree on the board showing two paths: either adjusting the audit strategy by increasing substantive testing, or seeking alternative evidence. Through a guided practice scenario, we simulate the impact of a qualified SOC 1 report where automated matching controls over sales billing were deemed ineffective. We show students that instead of panicking, the auditor must shift their audit approach to direct testing of receivables, demonstrating the direct operational connection between a third-party's IT controls and the scope of a year-end financial statement audit.

tasks: Identify essential complementary user entity controls (CUECs) for a payroll processing system.
Determine the audit impact of a qualified SOC report opinion.

exams.title: Information Systems and Controls (ISC) Discipline Exam
exams.goal: Verify proficiency in evaluating IT governance, analyzing system data flows, assessing cybersecurity risks, and auditing service provider SOC reports.
sections: Covers ERP structures, relational database schemas, logical access authorization, encryption, backup strategies, SOC Types 1 & 2, Trust Services Criteria, and user entity controls.
successCriteria: Interpret data flow diagrams and identify missing security controls.
Determine the correct SOC report type for a given scenario.
Design user access security matrix structures and verify backup processes.

units.title: Tax Compliance and Planning — TCP Discipline
units.description: Focuses on advanced individual and corporate tax planning, specialized entity compliance, gift and estate taxes, and tax research strategies.

lectures.title: Individual Tax Compliance and Planning
lectures.description: Advanced tax concepts for high-net-worth individuals, including complex equity compensation, investment vehicles, and retirement accounts.

sessions.title: Individual Tax Compliance
sessions.description: Study complex individual tax returns, net investment income tax (NIIT), and alternative minimum tax (AMT) computations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to today's session on complex individual tax compliance. Since our learner profile is geared toward a concept-first, public lecture style, we will build the theoretical frameworks of the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) and Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) from the ground up, using intuitive logical steps before executing quantitative calculations.

Let's start by introducing the fundamental purpose of the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT). On our virtual whiteboard, we want to sketch a dual-track tax system. On the left side, we have the Regular Income Tax system, and on the right side, we have the AMT system. The core concept to convey here is that AMT is a parallel tax system designed to ensure that high-income taxpayers who benefit from specific exclusions, deductions, and credits still pay a baseline share of tax. We want to visualize this as a 'floor' below which a taxpayer's liability cannot fall. To bridge the concept of Regular Taxable Income to Alternative Minimum Taxable Income (AMTI), we must illustrate the primary adjusting levers: positive adjustments (items that are added back because they are treated less favorably under AMT) and preference items (such as private activity bond interest). Explain to the class that a common pitfall is treating all regular tax deductions as AMT-allowable; for example, state and local taxes (SALT) are completely disallowed for AMT, which requires a full add-back.

Now, let's transition to the mathematical derivation of AMTI and the application of the AMT exemption. On the whiteboard, draft the equation: Regular Taxable Income +/- Adjustments + Preferences = AMTI. From AMTI, we subtract the AMT exemption, which is subject to a phase-out threshold based on high income. Walk through this phase-out mechanics visually with an escalating scale: show how as AMTI rises beyond the threshold, the exemption amount shrinks by 25 cents for every dollar over the limit, eventually reducing the exemption to zero. This sliding scale is a perfect touchpoint to show why moderately wealthy taxpayers sometimes face higher AMT exposures than ultra-wealthy individuals who have already completely phased out of the exemption. We will run a quick whiteboard practice problem: ask the students to identify a hypothetical client's status when state income tax paid is high, calculating the necessary add-back and checking if their AMTI triggers the phase-out.

Next, we pivot to the Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT), established under Internal Revenue Code Section 1411. On the whiteboard, draw a clear distinction between active earned income (like wages and active business income) and passive investment income. Introduce NIIT as a 3.8% surtax designed to target investment vehicles. Explain that the formula is a 'lesser of' evaluation: it applies to the lesser of the taxpayer's Net Investment Income (NII) OR the excess of their Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) over a statutory threshold (e.g., $250,000 for married filing jointly, $200,000 for single filers). Emphasize this logical fork because candidates often waste time calculating NIIT on the entire investment portfolio when the taxpayer's MAGI only slightly exceeds the threshold.

To solidify this, let us map out a combined analytical flowchart on the whiteboard. On one side, we track a taxpayer with substantial passive rental income and high MAGI, and on the other, a taxpayer with high W-2 wages but zero investment income. Walk through the decision nodes: Does the taxpayer have Net Investment Income? Yes. Is MAGI above the threshold? Yes. Calculate the excess MAGI, compare it to the total NII, and apply the 3.8% multiplier to the smaller bucket. Emphasize that municipal bond interest, while exempt from regular income tax, must be analyzed carefully; it is excluded from NII, preventing a common student error of including tax-exempt interest in the NIIT base. Conclude the session by contrasting these two parallel systems (AMT and NIIT), showing how they target different components of a high-net-worth individual's tax profile to protect the federal tax base.

tasks: Calculate alternative minimum taxable income (AMTI) adjustments.
Determine if a taxpayer is subject to the 3.8% net investment income tax.

sessions.title: Individual Tax Planning
sessions.description: Explore tax-minimization strategies, charitable giving structures, and passive activity loss planning.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by laying down the fundamental tension in tax planning: the distinction between active, portfolio, and passive income buckets. To make this concept-first approach resonate, visually sketch three distinct buckets on the board labeled 'Active' (salaries, wages), 'Portfolio' (dividends, interest, capital gains), and 'Passive' (rental activities, limited partnerships). The most critical conceptual takeaway here is that passive losses are generally ring-fenced; they cannot offset active or portfolio income. Explain the 'why' behind this legislative barrier—the historical context of tax shelters where high-earning individuals used artificial losses from passive investments to wipe out their active tax liabilities. Address a common student pitfall early: many assume that if they physically work on a rental property, it automatically makes the income active. Introduce the material participation tests briefly to show the high bar required to break out of the passive bucket.

Now, pivot to a real-world scenario to apply the passive activity loss (PAL) limitations. Draw an arrow representing a loss from a limited partnership interest on the board. Attempt to drag this loss into the portfolio bucket to offset capital gains from stock sales, and visually draw a large red 'X' through the path. This highlights the rule: passive losses can only offset passive income. Work through a calculation where a taxpayer has $15,000 of passive losses and only $5,000 of passive income. Show how $5,000 of the loss is consumed, while the remaining $10,000 is suspended and carried forward indefinitely. Emphasize that these suspended losses are not lost forever; they act as a tax bank account, waiting to offset future passive income or to be fully released when the taxpayer disposes of their entire interest in the activity in a fully taxable transaction.

Transition next to the strategic arena of charitable giving, contrasting cash contributions against gifts of appreciated capital gain property. On the left side of the whiteboard, draft a scenario where a high-net-worth individual wishes to make a $100,000 contribution using cash. Underneath, write out the tax consequences: they receive a deduction up to the applicable adjusted gross income (AGI) limitations (typically 60% for cash to public charities). On the right side, draft an alternative scenario where the taxpayer gifts stock worth $100,000 that they originally purchased for $10,000 (holding it for more than one year). 

This is where the magic of tax planning is visualized. Draw a dual-benefit flow chart. First, the taxpayer gets a charitable deduction for the full fair market value of $100,000 (subject to a 30% AGI limit for long-term capital gain property to public charities). Second, and more importantly, highlight that the $90,000 of untaxed built-in appreciation permanently escapes capital gains taxation. Contrast this with the common pitfall of selling the stock first and then donating the cash. Show that selling first triggers a massive capital gains tax bill, reducing the net tax benefit significantly. Guide the teacher to write down both pathways side-by-side to let students visually absorb the compounding power of tax-free growth avoidance.

Conclude the session with an interactive diagnostic check. Present a scenario where a taxpayer has a $20,000 loss from a rental property but also has $150,000 in portfolio dividend income. Ask the students to determine how much of the rental loss can be used to offset the dividend income. Use this to reveal if students are still falling for the temptation of mixing buckets or if they have internalized the absolute separation of passive and portfolio income. Wrap up by showing how planning is not about breaking the rules, but about restructuring transactions—such as shifting portfolios to generate passive income streams or timing asset sales—to legally and systematically minimize the overall tax drag.

tasks: Evaluate the tax benefit of gifting appreciated stock vs. cash.
Apply passive activity loss limits to offset portfolio income.

sessions.title: Compensation and Employee Benefits
sessions.description: Analyze tax implications for incentive stock options (ISOs), nonqualified stock options (NSOs), and restricted stock units (RSUs).
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core conceptual differences between equity compensation structures. For students approaching this without deep prior experience in tax mechanics, the central challenge is understanding 'when' tax events occur (grant, vest, exercise, or sale) and 'how' those events are characterized (ordinary income vs. capital gains). On the whiteboard, map out a horizontal timeline for a standard option life cycle. Use this timeline to define the two primary categories of employee stock options: Nonqualified Stock Options (NSOs) and Incentive Stock Options (ISOs). Explicitly show that NSOs trigger a dual tax event: first, an ordinary income event at exercise measured by the spread between the fair market value and the strike price, and second, a capital gains event at eventual sale. Contrast this visually by drawing the ISO timeline, highlighting that the exercise of an ISO triggers no immediate regular tax liability, shifting the entire tax event to the point of sale, provided holding periods are met. 

Next, dive into the mechanics of Restricted Stock Units (RSUs), which contrast sharply with stock options. On the whiteboard, illustrate that RSUs do not require an exercise decision. The vesting date is the single, critical focal point. Upon vesting, the fair market value of the shares is treated as ordinary wage income subject to FICA and income tax withholding. This is an opportune moment to address a high-frequency pitfall: students often confuse the vesting of RSUs with the vesting of stock options. For options, vesting merely grants the right to buy; it does not trigger a tax event. For RSUs, vesting is the tax event itself. Work through a clear calculation showing how an employer typically sells a portion of the vested shares on the spot ('sell-to-cover') to satisfy tax withholding requirements, leaving the employee with a net balance of shares. 

Now, introduce a comparative scenario on the board to solidify the tax calculations for ISOs and NSOs. Walk through a specific example: an employee is granted options to purchase 1,000 shares at a $10 strike price. At exercise, the stock is trading at $50. At sale, the stock is sold at $70. Draw the mathematical forks on the whiteboard. Under the NSO treatment, show how the $40 spread ($50 minus $10) creates $40,000 of ordinary income at exercise, establishing a new tax basis of $50 per share. Consequently, the sale at $70 triggers a $20 per share ($20,000 total) capital gain. For the ISO, show how the exercise generates $0 of regular taxable income, preserving the original $10 basis. Explain that when sold, the entire $60 spread ($70 minus $10) becomes a long-term capital gain of $60,000, assuming they met the holding period requirement of two years from grant and one year from exercise.

Immediately pivot to the critical 'gotcha' that candidates frequently overlook: the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) adjustment for ISO exercises. While ISO exercises are tax-free for regular tax purposes, the $40 spread in our scenario must be added back as an adjustment to Alternative Minimum Taxable Income (AMTI). On the whiteboard, draw the dual-track system: the regular tax track and the AMT track. Show how the AMT basis of the stock becomes $50, while the regular tax basis remains $10. Explain that if the stock price drops significantly before sale, the taxpayer can face a devastating situation where they owe AMT on phantom wealth they no longer possess. Explain how to monitor this exposure and how the subsequent sale of the ISO stock reverses this adjustment, creating an AMT capital gain that is smaller than the regular tax capital gain.

Conclude the session with an active learning checkpoint. Ask the class to evaluate a scenario where an employee exercises an ISO and sells the stock within six months, triggering a disqualifying disposition. Explain that this exercise reveals whether students understand that a disqualifying disposition collapses the ISO benefits, forcing the transaction to be taxed essentially like an NSO, with the spread at exercise recharacterized as ordinary income in the year of sale. Summarize the key takeaways on the board: NSOs yield ordinary income at exercise; RSUs yield ordinary income at vesting; ISOs yield capital gains at sale but require careful AMT tracking to avoid massive unexpected tax liabilities.

tasks: Compare the tax treatment of incentive stock options (ISOs) vs. nonqualified stock options (NSOs).
Calculate taxable wages upon the vesting of restricted stock units (RSUs).

sessions.title: Investment Taxation
sessions.description: Review wash sales, straddles, qualified business income (QBI) deductions, and capital gain tax planning.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by setting up a chronological timeline to address the mechanics of wash sales. Start by drawing a horizontal timeline spanning 60 days—specifically highlighting 30 days before and 30 days after a loss sale date. This visual anchor is critical because candidates frequently overlook the 'before' window, incorrectly assuming wash sales only trigger on subsequent purchases. Through this timeline, demonstrate how a disallowed loss does not disappear but is instead added to the basis of the newly acquired 'substantially identical' stock or security. This preserves the tax benefit for a future realization event. We will walk through a concrete example where an investor sells Stock A at a loss and repurchases it within the restricted window. Show the arithmetic of adjusting the new basis step-by-step on the board to illustrate how the tax deferral mechanism functions in practice.

Next, transition to tax straddles, shifting the whiteboard layout to a split-screen comparison of offsetting positions (such as matching call and put options). Explain that the core policy objective here is to prevent taxpayers from accelerating losses while deferring matching gains. On the board, sketch a scenario where a taxpayer holds straddle positions with unrealized gains on one side and realized losses on the other. Draw connection lines demonstrating how the loss must be deferred to the extent of any unrecognized gain at the end of the tax year. Point out the common pitfall of forgetting to track the character of the loss (capital vs. ordinary) and show how the straddle rules affect holding periods, which can reset to zero when offsetting positions are established.

From individual transaction rules, we scale up to the business-level planning side by introducing the Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction under Section 199A. Draw a conceptual block diagram showing the flow of QBI from a pass-through entity to an individual's Form 1040. The first major concept to establish is the basic 20% deduction limit and how it is restricted by the taxpayer’s taxable income thresholds. Highlight that for taxpayers below the threshold, the calculation is straightforward, but as taxable income rises, a complex phase-out system is triggered based on the type of business—Specifically Designated Trade or Business (SSTB) versus Qualified Trade or Business (QTB).

To make the QBI phase-out intuitive, draw a vertical 'Phase-out Zone' ladder on the board. On this ladder, map out the W-2 wage and Qualified Property (UBIA) limitation formulas. Guide the students through a step-by-step calculation where a taxpayer's income falls right in the middle of the phase-out range for a QTB. Write out the formulas side-by-side: first, the un-limited 20% of QBI; second, the alternative limit based on 50% of W-2 wages (or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of UBIA). Show how the phase-out fraction reduces the deduction from the tentative 20% down to the wage-limited amount. Emphasize that for SSTBs, the deduction completely vanishes once taxable income exceeds the upper threshold. This visual representation prevents students from getting lost in the arithmetic by grounding them in the policy intent of restricting high-earning service providers from claiming the deduction.

Conclude the session with an active learning scenario that synthesizes wash sales and QBI planning. Ask the students to analyze a taxpayer who wants to harvest tax losses from their investment portfolio to offset high ordinary income, while simultaneously planning for a year-end QBI deduction. On the board, trace how capital losses can only offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income for individuals, and how minimizing adjusted gross income (AGI) through these losses can actually help keep the taxpayer below the QBI phase-out threshold. This final synthesis highlights how investment taxation decisions directly impact broader individual planning metrics, reinforcing a holistic approach to the CPA discipline-level material.

tasks: Calculate disallowed losses under the 30-day wash sale rules.
Apply phase-out limitations to a taxpayer's QBI deduction.

sessions.title: Retirement Planning
sessions.description: Examine traditional vs. Roth accounts, required minimum distributions (RMDs), and rollover mechanics.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by drawing a stark vertical line down the center of the board to establish the fundamental tax divergence in retirement planning: Traditional vs. Roth. The goal of this visual setup is to anchor the timing of tax benefits. Under the Traditional umbrella, we write 'Pre-Tax Contributions' and 'Taxed Distributions', representing a tax deferral mechanism. On the Roth side, we write 'Post-Tax Contributions' and 'Tax-Free Distributions', representing tax-free growth. We must emphasize the core tax planning thesis: the choice between these vehicles is a game of predictive tax rate arbitrage. If a client expects their tax rate to be higher in retirement, Roth is the clear winner; if they expect a lower tax rate, Traditional wins. We want to explicitly point out a high-frequency student pitfall here: many mistakenly assume Roth accounts are always superior because of the tax-free distributions, completely overlooking the present-value impact of giving up immediate tax deductions when the taxpayer is currently in their peak earning years.

Next, we transition to the mechanics of direct Roth IRA contribution eligibility, which requires a step-by-step mathematical ladder drawn on the board. We will write out the Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) phase-out ranges clearly, highlighting that these thresholds change annually based on filing status (Single vs. Married Filing Jointly). On the whiteboard, we will sketch a graph where the horizontal axis represents MAGI and the vertical axis represents the allowable contribution limit, showing a downward-sloping linear phase-out. We will walk through an example of a single taxpayer whose income falls right in the middle of the phase-out range. The mathematical calculation of the reduced contribution limit must be derived step-by-step: subtracting the lower limit from MAGI, dividing by the range width, and multiplying by the maximum allowable contribution to find the disallowed portion. This visual and formulaic approach ensures students understand that eligibility is not an all-or-nothing binary switch, but a progressive scale.

Moving to the other end of the retirement lifecycle, we introduce the mechanics of early withdrawals and their associated penalties. On the whiteboard, we will draw a 'Distributions Flowchart'. We will write down the golden age '59½' and outline the general rule: early distributions from qualified plans are subject to ordinary income tax plus a 10% penalty. To build deep intuition, we will write down the primary statutory exceptions as 'escape hatches' from the 10% penalty, such as death, disability, qualified first-time homebuyer expenses (capped at $10,000), and qualified higher education expenses. We will run through a practical calculation scenario: a 40-year-old taxpayer withdrawing $30,000 from a traditional IRA for non-qualified personal use. We will visually separate the tax liability calculation ($30,000 multiplied by their marginal tax rate) from the penalty calculation (10% of $30,000) to ensure students do not make the common mistake of applying the 10% penalty to the net-of-tax distribution amount, or forgetting that the penalty applies on top of, not instead of, ordinary income tax.

Finally, we will address rollover mechanics and Required Minimum Distributions (RMDs) to round out the planning framework. On the whiteboard, we will map out the '60-Day Indirect Rollover' versus the 'Direct Trustee-to-Trustee Transfer' using arrow diagrams. We must clearly highlight the danger of the 60-day rule: the 20% withholding tax on indirect rollovers from employer-sponsored plans often catches taxpayers off guard, creating a phantom income tax event if they fail to deposit the full gross amount (including the withheld 20% using outside funds) into the new account within the 60-day window. We will close by writing the formula for RMDs, highlighting how the account balance is divided by the IRS Life Expectancy factor, and emphasizing the severe penalty for failing to take an RMD on time. This leaves students with a complete, structured visual guide to advising clients on the accumulation, maintenance, and distribution phases of retirement assets.

tasks: Calculate tax and penalty liabilities for early retirement account withdrawals.
Determine eligibility limits for direct Roth IRA contributions.

sessions.title: Personal Financial Planning Considerations
sessions.description: Integrate education savings accounts (529 plans), HSA treatments, and life insurance vehicles into tax plans.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core mechanics of tax-advantaged accounts, specifically contrasting the growth of standard brokerage accounts with the triple tax advantages of 529 Qualified Tuition Programs and Health Savings Accounts (HSAs). The goal here is to establish a concept-first public lecture framework that bridges the gap between everyday wealth management and high-yield CPA Tax Compliance and Planning (TCP) concepts. We will draw a simple timeline on the whiteboard showing an initial contribution, a holding period of tax-free growth, and a distribution phase. This visual representation allows students to instantly see where taxes are bypassed compared to a standard taxable brokerage account, where annual drag from dividends, capital gains, and interest payments occurs. 

We then dive deep into 529 plans, tracing the logical path from state-level tax incentives to federal tax-free growth. On the whiteboard, we map out the contribution limits (and the unique 5-year gift tax front-loading election, or 'superfunding'), the investment growth phase, and the qualified distribution rules. To help learners avoid a very common pitfall, we explicitly highlight the difference between qualified education expenses (such as tuition, fees, books, and up to $10,000 of student loan repayments) and non-qualified expenses. We will run through a quick scenario where a parent mistakenly uses 529 funds for general travel expenses, illustrating how the earnings portion of that distribution is subjected to both regular income tax and a 10% penalty. This contrast reinforces the critical regulatory boundaries of qualified educational costs.

Next, we transition to Health Savings Accounts (HSAs), which offer a unique triple-tax advantage: pre-tax contributions, tax-free growth, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified medical expenses. On the whiteboard, we write out the requirements for HSA eligibility, emphasizing that the taxpayer must be enrolled in a High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP). We will list what constitutes a 'qualified medical expense' (including doctor visits, prescriptions, and dental care) versus non-qualified items. To deepen understanding, we will walk through a tactical practice exercise comparing a $5,000 medical expense paid out of pocket versus using tax-free HSA funds. This exercise demonstrates how HSAs function as an investment vehicle rather than just a medical spending account, as unused balances roll over indefinitely and can even be invested in equities to defer taxes long-term.

Finally, we integrate these concepts by analyzing how life insurance vehicles, such as cash-value policies, fit into a high-net-worth individual's holistic financial and tax plan. We will outline the tax treatment of policy loans (which are generally non-taxable) and death benefits (which are income tax-free to the beneficiary). By visualizing the interaction of 529 plans, HSAs, and life insurance on the whiteboard, we wrap up the session by demonstrating how an advisor balances these distinct vehicles to maximize tax efficiency, protect assets, and secure multi-generational wealth.

tasks: Evaluate the tax benefits of 529 plan contributions vs. standard brokerage accounts.
Identify qualified medical expenses for tax-free HSA distributions.

lectures.title: Entity Tax Compliance and Planning
lectures.description: Examines corporate, partnership, and estate tax compliance, and addresses entity choice, creation, distributions, and liquidations.

sessions.title: C Corporation Compliance
sessions.description: Study consolidated tax returns, net operating loss (NOL) limitations, and international tax reporting.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the core structure of consolidated tax returns, a critical regulatory mechanism for affiliated corporate groups. Rather than presenting this as a series of disparate filing rules, we will use a visual organizational chart on the whiteboard to illustrate the definition of an affiliated group under Section 1504, highlighting the 80% voting power and value test. The fundamental concept here is that a consolidated return treats the affiliated group as a single economic entity while respecting individual legal corporate structures. Teachers should explain that transactions between member corporations—such as intercompany sales or dividend distributions—must be systematically eliminated to prevent double counting.
